OTTAWA TORCH DAT CEREMONY ON PARLIAMENT HILL ON WEDNESDAY, JUNE 11
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the house that I have received the following communication:
Office of the Mayor Ottawa, Canada
4th June, 1941.
Hon. J. A. Glen,
Speaker of the House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Victory Loan 1941 Dear Mr. Glen:
The torch and scroll being carried by air force bomber from Victoria to Halifax and thence to England to be presented to the Right Hon. Winston Churchill will arrive in Ottawa on the 11th June. The Ottawa torch day ceremony will take place on that day on parliament hill at 5 o'clock.
At the ceremony the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King will be the speaker and arrangements are being made for His Excellency the Governor General, the Right Hon. the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and myself to sign the scroll.
On behalf of the committee I have the honour to invite you to attend this ceremony. I beg to request also that you will extend an invitation to the members of the House of Commons to be present.
Sincerely yours,
J. E. S. Lewis,
Mayor.

May I ask the Prime Minister whether we are to sit to-night and/or to-morrow? If we are to sit to-night, why not to-morrow, and if we are not to sit to-morrow, why sit to-night?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I shall try to answer my hon. friend as logically as I can. First of all we are sitting in the mornings in order to get through the business of this part of the session as soon as possible. For that reason we are sitting afternoons and evenings as well. Therefore I think it would be well for the house to continue sitting this afternoon and this evening.
In regard to to-morrow, the reason we do not propose to sit this Saturday is that it has -been thought by the government, and was so stated in the house some weeks ago, that it would be eminently fitting that the fiftieth anniversary of the death of Sir John A. Macdonald should be made the occasion of a national recognition of the memory of Sir John A. Macdonald. To-day is the fiftieth anniversary of Sir John's death. The special services in commemoration of the anniversary have been arranged to take place at Kingston to-morrow at which the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) and myself, and I hope many of his colleagues and of mine and members of the house generally, will be present. For that reason the house will not be sitting to-morrow.
I do not know whether my hon. friend said anything about Monday, but I think it continues to be the wish of hon. members to conclude as early as possible this part of the session; therefore I would think we should continue sitting on Monday morning, afternoon and night.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MILLERS' ASSOCIATION AS TO GRISTED WHEAT
speechtext:
I have a question I should like to address to the Minister of Trade and Commerce of which I gave him notice. It arises out of a telegram I have received from the Saskat-

Gristed Wheat
chewan Flour Millers' Association in reference to the wheat policy of the government. The telegram reads as follows:
The wheat policy tabled in the house on Friday by Trade Minister Hon. Mr. MacKinnon compels the farmers gristing their wheat for their own family use to take same out of their wheat quota which will be very small to start with and will not give most of them enough cash to buy the necessities required for their families. If they have to take the wheat from their quota that will cut in further to their small cash allowance if they are allowed to grist their year's supply of flour it will be wonderful help to them as they will get their flour and feed much cheaper than if they had to buy. Most of the small mills are depending mostly on the gristing trade for their business and if the farmers are discouraged in their gristing that means that most of the small mills will have to shut down their plants. We are sorry it has been said that some of the small millers did bootlegging on gristing and flour sales to avoid the processing tax. If the Hon. Mr. MacKinnon will instruct the wheat board to consult with our executive when making their rules and regulations for 41-42 crop we will make watertight suggestions.
D. G. McLean,
Executive Member, Saskatchewan Flour Millers' Association.
Is the minister prepared to consider the changes suggested by the millers' association, and what assurances will he give in that regard?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: MILLERS' ASSOCIATION AS TO GRISTED WHEAT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Lake Centre gave me ample notice of his intention to ask this question and gave me the opportunity to discuss the matter with my officials Who are in Ottawa at the present time.
The quantity of wheat which can be delivered by the producer in the whole of Canada this coming crop year has been limited to 230,000,000 bushels. This figure has been made up of approximately 50,000,000 bushels for human consumption in Canada and approximately 180,000,000 bushels for export. It will be necessary that on any wheat gristed the amount gristed will have to be taken out of the farmers' wheat quota, because to the extent that this was not done, the 50,000,000 bushels for domestic consumption would have to be reduced. In other words all of the Wheat gristed for human use is a part of the 50,000,000 bushels, and if it was not deducted from his quota, the producer who had his wheat gristed would have an advantage over those who were not able to have their wheat gristed and would be able to deliver a relatively higher proportion than his neighbouring farmer. There would be discrimination between farmers.
Any amount of wheat gristed in this way would be a deduction from the 50,000,000 bushels and would increase the carryover to the same extent, which is contrary to the intention of the order in council.
I may say that I have arranged this morning with the wheat board to meet with the Saskatchewan Flour Millers' association immediately on their return to the west, when these matters can be discussed. Further consideration is also being given.

Labour Department Act

LABOUR DEPARTMENT ACT amendment to provide for the appointment

Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Minister of Labour) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Labour Department Act to provide for the appointment of an associate deputy minister of Labour.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Yien in the chair.

I think we should have from the minister a complete statement, although not necessarily a long one, as to the necessity of the appointment of an additional deputy minister. I appreciate the fact that with the increased business and present unsettled state of things another deputy minister may be necessary. I would point out, however, having been around here for twenty years, that if you create a new position like this, carrying with it a substantial salary, the probabilities are that it will be a permanent one. There is never any going back when public offices of the kind are created; it is claimed thereafter as a matter of right. The minister should justify the appointment, and if it is of a temporary nature, it should be so stated. We have had a number of new deputy ministers in the defence portfolio. Of course we agree that they are necessary under the circumstances. But in this case there should be some undertaking on the part of the government that hereafter and for all time to come we are not to be burdened with two deputy ministers of labour.

The work of the Department of Labour has been very greatly increased in the last two years. In the first place the purpose of this bill-because the present associate deputy minister has been appointed- is to make his appointment permanent rather than temporary.
The work of the department has been greatly expanded in three directions: in the first place, in the wide extension of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act; in the second place, in the passing of the Unemployment Insurance Act; in the third place, through the war emergency training plan.
The Department of Labour has, I believe, always had a minimum of help for the wide work it has to do. We have appointed as associate deputy minister Mr. MacNamara, former deputy minister of labour and public works in the province of Manitoba. He has been acting since the regrettable death of Doctor Sirois as acting chief commissioner of

the Unemployment Insurance Act. The salary which the leader of the opposition refers to as being large is not really large when you consider the administrative ability which the present incumbent as Associate Deputy Minister of Labour has brought to bear in the organization of the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is because of this wide extension of the definite functions of the Department of Labour that the appointment of an associate deputy minister is necessary and desirable. I need hardly say that Mr. MacNamara is carrying on his task in an excellent way and doing splendid work in promoting the early introduction of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
What is the salary?

$9,000. I do not believe it is excessive. In my opinion it is justified by . the added responsibilities placed upon the Department of Labour; and may I suggest that there will be even greater responsibilities after the war is over. In view of all these considerations I believe it will be agreed that the appointment of an associate deputy minister is desirable.

I agree
with what the minister has said respecting the administrative ability of Mr. MacNamara. He is a man who had wide experience in another field when he came here to head the dependents' allowance board. I am satisfied he did excellent work when he was promoted, if that is the proper expression, to the office of acting head of the unemployment insurance commission. I had hoped the minister and the government would see their way clear to appoint him permanently to that position in place of Mr. Sirois. Apparently, however, that is not now the proposal, and the position is to be filled otherwise.
Let us for a moment examine the bases of the minister's proposal. He has given as a first reason the wide extension of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. What I believe he meant was the wide extension of the operations of that act, because so far as I know there is to be no wide extension of the principles underlying the act. Certainly it is not indicated in the bill the minister is to bring before the house. I had hoped that the wide extension in the operation of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act would be purely temporary. It is hoped by everyone that these labour troubles which from day to day have been looming up on the horizon, and growing more extensive, will by the exercise of good-will and judgment, and by conference, be reduced to a minimum. That, I suggest, is a temporary

Labour Department Act
position only. Surely it is not sufficient reason for appointing a new permanent associate deputy minister, who would be here for all time in that capacity.
The second ground upon which the minister has based the decision to appoint this new officer is the establishment of the Unemployment Insurance Act. The organization operating under that measure will of course be a permanent institution. I should have hoped that in the operation of the act the commission would be the responsible body, and that they could report through ordinary channels, namely, to the deputy minister of labour, and through the deputy minister to the minister and the house. That in itself would not necessitate any great increase in the burden of work devolving upon the Department of Labour. Surely this commission is in large measure to be independent of the Department of Labour. The administrative sections of the act contemplate independence. It is to be a commission, not a bureau of the Department of Labour and, so far as possible, it is to act independently of that department, only reporting through it to the government. So that the second ground upon which the minister justifies the appointment falls down.
His third ground, namely, the setting up of a trade training plan, is in my view the least substantial of all. Surely that is a war measure -at least I so understand it. That is the basis upon which it was introduced and upon which it has been so far operated. It is not contemplated, I hope, that the federal government will permanently go into what is primarily a provincial field, namely that of education. As I understand it, this plan has been adopted on the theory that we have not enough mechanics for our war effort. That is a reasonable view to take, but 'it is an ephemeral thing; it is not to last forever. I suggest the minister will have to justify the creation of this new position on some higher ground.
What is to be done with the chairmanship of the unemployment insurance commission? Is somebody else to be appointed to do that work? So far as I know Mr. MacNamara is performing very satisfactorily the duties of that office, and unless there is some objection to his appointment as chairman of the commission, he should be confirmed in that position. In my view the minister has not justified the creation of a second deputy minister of labour, who would be a permanent official of the government. If we are to have two deputy ministers, which is to be the senior? Which is to have overriding jurisdiction? Are they to be on equal planes? What is to happen if they disagree? Or is it desired not to appoint Mr. MacNamara to the chairmanship of the unemployment insurance commission, but to obtain his very valuable services in some high executive capacity? Does this resolution contain that principle? At the moment I must conclude the minister has not justified his proposal.

There are a few observations which I should like to make on this resolution and also in respect of the other bill on the order paper in the name of the Minister of Labour. Most of what I wish to say I shall reserve until second reading.
Certainly this group will not oppose a resolution which has for its purpose the strengthening of the administration of the Department of Labour. About two months ago I drew the attention of the house to the serious conditions developing in industry throughout the country, and I insisted at that time that something should be done about it. On that occasion the Minister of Labour took exception to my remarks and indicated that everything was quiet on the industrial front. In view of certain actions he has taken in the last few days, and in view of questions which have been asked in the house and reports appearing in the press, I suggest he would have been well advised to accept my opinion and become more active at that time. However, better late than never.
I am always amazed when, on almost every question brought up in the house, the leader of the opposition asks, "Is this just for the duration?" His question seems to me to indicate a lack of understanding of what is happening in the world to-day. When I hear him speak in that way I am reminded of two legendary characters which I liked to read about in my youth. One was in the biblical story of the patriarch Lot. We remember that in the flight from Sodom, at the time of that city's destruction, Lot's wife insisted on looking back, with the result that she was turned into a pillar of salt. Again, I am reminded of Rip Van Winkle, in Washington Irving's classic "Sleepy Hollow," who slept for twenty years. I am convinced, however, that the leader of the opposition reminds me more of Lot's wife, because Rip Van Winkle did eventually wake up.
There are certain developments taking place to-day which we cannot ignore even if we would. We cannot ignore the fact that we have fewer and larger industries in this country under the control of fewer people and employing a greater number of wage-earners. This creates an industrial problem which the government will have to prepare to meet in the same way as it has organized to meet its foreign problem, its trade and commerce problem, and in fact its war prob-
Labour Department Act

lem or any other problems that may confront us. Unless we can find some way to turn the clock back to the primitive production which existed in this country in 1867, the Department of Labour will have to be strengthened. Its administrative functions will increase to meet increasing demands, and wisdom would indicate that we should organize to meet these increased demands.
I am pleased that the minister has taken this step at this time. While we may have some detailed criticism to make later, we are not opposing the measure; in fact we approve this resolution.

I am quite opposed to the suggestion attributed to me by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. The Department of Labour should be strengthened, but it should not be made top-heavy. What is the position to-day? We have the minister with a salary of $10,000; up to this year we had a deputy minister with a salary of $8,000, and we had an assistant with a salary of $5,220. That was the set-up until Mr. Stewart was introduced as deputy minister. My understanding is that he is a high-class man who came into the department, perhaps against his will, and insisted upon a salary of $10,000.
At some sacrifice.

At some sacrifice, I believe. It is not known definitely whether he will make this his permanent vocation. That made a total of $23,220 for the three executive heads. But what have we to-day? We have the minister at $10,000, the deputy minister at $10,000, an associate deputy minister at $9,000, an assistant deputy minister at $5,220, and an executive assistant to the minister, whatever that may be, at $4,200. The total salary cost is $38,420, as opposed to the previous establishment which cost $23,220.
I want to elucidate these facts for the benefit of the taxpayers. Here is a non-war portfolio, which may be associated with the war effort along certain lines. It is agreed that there are temporary added responsibilities, but after this war is over, unless somebody gives consideration to this position, we will have for all time executives at the head of the Department of Labour costing $38,000. In addition a man is to be appointed to head the unemployment insurance commission at a salary of $12,000. I am calling attention to what has taken place in order that the people of Canada may know. We are being asked to tighten our belts, to give and lend to the government, and at the same time we are running away with executive expenditures.

That is all I have to say about this matter. I cannot stop it, because the appointment is an accomplished fact. This appointee is already in the department, and, as the minister has said, this is simply to legalize what has been done already by executive action. I think the appointment is a good one; this gentleman will do excellent work, but let us understand the proposal and what it means. Hereafter the Department of Labour is to have five executive heads instead of three.

It is difficult to come to one's feet after the leader of the opposition has spoken, but I cannot but think of the Department of Labour to-day and the Department of Labour when the present Prime Minister was its deputy minister. I cannot but think of the Department of Labour under the late Hon. Norman Rogers. I have been surprised that another deputy minister has not been appointed before this. I ask the leader of the opposition how much the Department of National Defence is costing to-day as compared with what it cost before the war. I am one of those who take the stand that this government must wake up. It must keep alive the work that was started by the late Hon. Norman Rogers, something which I think the Minister of Labour is doing. The appointment of an associate deputy minister is long overdue, but I suggest that this deputy minister be a man who understands labour, who has come up from the ranks of labour and knows what a hard day's work at no great pay feels like. I think of the time I spent helping the late Hon. Norman Rogers with the youth training work. I could see then the magnitude of the task. This is one side of labour to which a man could devote his whole time. This type of work may not be needed to-day as much as it was during the years of the depression, and as it will be after the war, but it is still important. I hope to see the dominion government take over the whole problem of relief. If that is done, the work of this department will be increased and additional experts will be needed.
I repeat that this deputy minister should know labour. While the heads of our government departments may know something about these matters, I am afraid the public at large do not appreciate the problems of labour. If labour is happy, the country will be happy. I do not agree with the leader of the opposition when he says that there will be a great depression after this war. I believe that if this country can raise $5,000,000 a day for war, we can raise enough to cure unemployment and develop our resources. If the Department of Labour can lead in this endeavour, then we say, "Go to it and we will give you our support."

Labour Department Act

Mention has been made of a salary of $12,000 per annum, but I would direct attention to resolution No. 12 which stands on the order paper in my name, and which suggests that for the duration of the war any government salary which exceeds $10,000 should be reduced to one dollar per annum plus $10 per day for living expenses. The suggestion is made to appoint an associate deputy minister of labour. In the Department of Labour as at present constituted there are three competent persons, the minister, his private sjcretary and the young lady who works in his office-the rest is nil. It is pitiful, and I mentioned this to the late Hon. Norman Rogers when he was alive. I am not discussing the excellent work done by my chief when he was deputy minister of labour and minister of labour. But he ceased to be Minister of Labour in 1911, and since then there have been many other ministers of labour whom I do not discuss. Some have been good, some bad, and some have been nonentities. The present minister is a good one. But I am strongly opposed to any salary in excess of $10,000 being paid. I think that that amount is enough, and when one man in the department receives $10,000 I do not see why another one should be paid as much as that. I think it is a scandal to appoint a man at over $10,000. There is not a man who is worth more than that in these hard times-unless he strikes a gold mine.
The suggestion has been made to take someone from the ranks of labour for this position. The suggestion has come from our reverend and very dear colleague from Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), who is perhaps one of the most popular members of the House of Commons. My experience with labour is that there are two kinds of labour men, those who work and those who do not.
Like members of parliament.

Exactly, but that is true of very walk of life. Those who call themselves labour are those who do nothing and receive big salaries, and who are not working for labour men-they are company men. I have demonstrated that very often in this house, and I warn the minister against the appointment of any impostor of the kind, any lobbyist who calls himself labour to get a fat job and a salary ten times what he could earn with his own hands. Some people are under the impression that if we have no strikes in this country it is due to one man alone, a man you must see eating if you want to see him at work because that is the only work he does, with a knife and fork and spoon. There
was a rumour at one time that he was to be put on the purchasing board. I asked the minister for air and the minister for health, is this man going to be on the board? They looked embarrassed, and I knew then that it was only a rumour and that this man had not been asked. He has been mentioned as a possibility as minister, and here again when I occupied the seat in this chamber in which the Minister of Labour now sits I warned the government against his appointment, at the same time acknowledging that the Prime Minister had the right to choose anyone he liked, but stating that I could not support as one of my chiefs a man like that. He was not appointed. My friend who was the Postmaster General was appointed in his stead.
I am after this man because I think he is a fake, that he has betrayed labour, that he is an impostor, that he is a "Purvis" man in labour. Everybody knows him. I strongly object to his appointment. He has betrayed labour. He is only a lobbyist, an intriguer of the worst type.
May we know to whom the hon. member is referring?
If my hon. friend does not know he is not well informed.
I do not know.

If my hon. friend listened to my speeches he would know. If instead of making a noise when I speak he would listen to what I say he would be better informed.
Here we are, $12,000 for that man. It is a scandal. I denounce it because the man is an impostor, because the man calls himself labour when he has no right to call himself labour, when he has cost the country thousands and thousands, scores of thousands of dollars, to travel to places like Geneva where he has done nothing. He did not say anything, no more than a fish could say in water. He had nothing to say, and here is the man who represents labour. If I were a labour man I would be ashamed to be represented by an impostor of that kind-and when a man is successful enough to reach his post through intrigue he must be exposed as is and must be hanged on the next post. What I say I know. I warn the house about him all the time, but it is of no use. I remember that one of the members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party who holds a big job in that department got it through him because every time I denounced that impostor he was defended by that Cooperative Commonwealth Federation member in the house, and that man
Labour Department Act

rewarded the member by getting him a fat job. Everybody knows he is an impostor as I have described.
I do not want to say any more because then he would pose as a martyr. He will say I am crucifying a labour man, that I have no respect for labour. I know the labour men perhaps as well as any man in this house, if not better, and labour men are not afraid to speak to me or to come to me and ask me to defend their rights. When I have a big fat obstacle of the kind in my way I want to get rid of it, and I do the same as a man would who is driving along the road and sees a dead log blocking his path. He takes it away and throws it in the ditch so that he can proceed.
These are my humble views, and I warn the Minister of Labour, who is my friend, and tell him that if this appointment is made- he knows my reasons-it will be a bad appointment, and he will have to establish a cafeteria next to the man's office-

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, but I must say that I do not think he is referring to the associate deputy minister of labour. I am not sure whom he is referring to and I wonder if he would make that clear.

The best way to conclude is to tell the minister immediately whom I have in view and then he will know if my remarks apply to that man. I do not want the labour men of this country to be betrayed. I want them to be defended by someone who is true to them and who has not changed his mind to get a big salary.

Mr. Chairman, I always listen with a great deal of interest to what the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) says, but this morning we have listened to a speech made in a very general way about an unnamed person. In my opinion if an attack is going to be made on an individual connected with any labour organization, it should be made on a particular individual and reasons should be advanced for the attack. I think I know perfectly well the gentleman to whom the hon. member intended to refer.
Who is he?

I want simply to say this, that the man who has been attacked without being named is one who has held for a number of years the highest office in the larger of our two national labour organizations. I refer to Mr. Tom Moore. I would say this, that a man who has held the trust
[Mr. Pouliot.!
of such a large section of organized labour cannot by any stretch of the imagination be an impostor of the type the hon. member for Temiscouata would have us believe he is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should like to point out that I thought the hon. member for Temiscouata would come to naming the man to whom he was referring. The Minister of Labour, when discussing this position, stated that the man intended for it was Mr. MacNamara, at present acting chairman of the unemployment insurance commission. Therefore I think it would be quite improper and out of order to continue the discussion on the merits or demerits of a man who had not been named for the position. I would have stopped the hon. member for Temiscouata had I not thought that he would name the man, because the committee must realize that there can be no discussion about some one who is not named.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but I do not think it is the right or the privilege of any member to make an assumption and arrive at a conclusion as to what the minister intends to do, nor do I believe it is the prerogative of any member to throw down the gage of battle with a minister of the crown and to tell him that if he does certain things, then something unpleasant may happen either here or elsewhere. It was with that thought in mind that I rose. I am quite sure that in these difficult times when the Minister of Labour makes an appointment, no matter who the appointee may be, he will choose some one who will have the confidence of organized labour, in spite of anything that any member of this house may think privately of the person so appointed. I have no doubt that when he appoints an assistant deputy minister of labour he will look round the country and choose someone who is known to have the confidence of organized labour. Every member of this house, I believe, was aware of the identity of the gentleman at whom the remarks were directed, because he has been named by the member for Temiscouata before. 1 felt I could not allow this occasion to pass without expressing the opinion that the attack was most unfair and unjustified.

One word on a question of principle. I find the doctrine expressed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar absurd. A member of parliament has the right not only to criticize what the government has done, but to give warning, and my hon. friend knows that. If he who is an advocate of free speech says that I cannot give a warning to the minister just to help him, perhaps he would

Labour Department Act
like the minister to make a bad appointment so as to have other opportunities to criticize him afterwards. I give the minister an opportunity to think before something is done, and I express my views and tell the government what I think. I have a right to do so and the member for Rosetown-Biggar will not deny it.
I don't.
That is all I want. If the minister mentioned Mr. MacNamara, I did not have him in view in what I said.

The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), in the few remarks he made, stated the position of this group. I am not going to say anything with regard to the remarks of the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). I know not to whom he refers, but I do think it is absolutely unfair to make insinuations and to accuse someone in a general way, which might very well be construed as meaning someone connected with the labour movement. I feel as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar does. If a man is to be attacked he should be named, the charge made, and the cards laid on the table face up, so that he may be in a position to defend himself. That is all I have to say in that regard.
I am concerned about the attitude of the leader of the opposition. He classifies the Department of Labour as a non-war department. I have exactly the opposite view. I believe that many of the troubles we are confronted with to-day in regard to strikes, and all the general confusion resulting, are due to the fact that the Department of Labour, constituted as it is, is totally inadequate to handle a situation which it was not organized to deal with on a peace-time basis. It is the most essential war department in the government. I am altogether in accord with the steps taken by the minister to strengthen the department. The discussion with regard to salaries and such matters might very well be dispensed with at this time. Certainly it is not good war propaganda to have members stand up and talk about salaries of $10,000 and $20,000, whpn we realize that perhaps 95 per cent of the men we are calling to take up a gun and defend the country might compare income tax brackets. This sort of thing is all bad propaganda and should be discontinued. I am saying nothing about salaries. I have always been of the opinion that they are absolutely out of proportion to the earnings or wages of the people who, when all is said, produce the wealth of the country.
I think our whole set-up of war departments has been handled in the wrong way. In the
first place, the hon. member objects to an additional deputy minister in the Department of Labour where the work has increased a hundredfold since the outbreak of war. He-fails to realize that the country has been transformed and is now on a war-time basis. The department must therefore be prepared to meet the crisis. We have established additional branches in the Department of National Defence. For instance, we have the ministry for naval services. That is not necessary in peace time but it is indispensable to-day. We have a ministry for air, with a personnel scattered across the country. All this involves expenditures, but these branches are absolutely necessary.
The Department of Labour is the most important war department of the government, because it deals exclusively with the men and women necessary to produce the sinews of war. The army and the navy are worth nothing unless our industries are so organized and planned that they will turn out the necessary machinery for these forces to enable them to fight the battle we are engaged in. In the organization of some 35 or 40 boards the personnel in each case has been drawn from one class. These people have but one outlook, and the point of view of labour is given no consideration in any of the organizations that function behind the government in organizing the war effort. The result is that the whole establishment is influenced by a single point of view. This has its repercussions throughout the country in the turmoil and unrest we are having. The Minister of Labour would do well to bring into the department men who have knowledge of both sides of the picture, men who are qualified to sit in, and whose advice would tend to alleviate some of the disturbance we have to-day simply because of the fact that only one point of view prevails.
I am absolutely in agreement with what the minister is doing. I have no jurisdiction over salaries and I am not going to talk about them. That is a departmental matter, and if the government think it good business I recognize my limitations. I think we on this side of the house should withhold any statements in the house which might have a reaction outside that would not be in the best interests of the country.
As the hon. member for Vancouver East stated, later we may have something more to say with respect to matters concerning the Department of Labour. But that is my feeling at the present time. We have to have both points of view represented on the inside in all these matters, because I regard the Department of Labour as the most important war organization we have. I sympathize with the
Labour Department Act

minister in respect of the many problems with which he has to deal; they have increased from day to day. It should be our duty to assist him to strengthen the department in every way possible, and I am prepared to do that.
Mr. O'NEILL: This debate has taken a rather wide range; we have been discussing salaries and more or less personalities. As a labour man I have never been one to question salaries, but it seems to me that there could be a redistribution of the amount of money that is paid in any one department. If it is not possible to raise the salaries of those who are getting less than a living wage without taking something off the $10,000 man, then probably something of the kind should be done. That, however, is not what I wish to discuss at present.
It seems to me that this measure for the appointment of an additional deputy minister in the Department of Labour is looked upon by some hon. members from the point of view that it should be a war time measure only. The Department of Agriculture is probably the most important department in the government and I think next in importance is the Department of Labour. I am entirely in agreement with this resolution. It is my view that an associate deputy minister of labour should be appointed and that he should be retained after the war, because then we shall have problems arising in the labour world that will require a great deal of attention, and these men should be in the department now making provision to meet the troubles that will come upon us when the war is over.
Another thing that perhaps has not been given the consideration by the government that it should have is with respect to the appointment of the men to fill these positions. If the government wish to use the democratic method in appointing men to positions in the Department of Labour-and take note that I do not wish to be misconstrued as having anything against Mr. MacNamara; I have nothing whatsoever against him-it should have' in mind the fact that a deputy minister or associate deputy minister of labour should have the respect and confidence of labour. We have labour organizations in this country. We have the standard labour organizations on the railways, about eighteen of them holding contracts with the railways. We have the trades and labour congress, the Canadian congress of labour, the Canadian federation of labour, the Catholic workers of Quebec, and so on. All these labour organizations have their heads. If it is desired to have a
[Mr. GillisJ
man who has the respect and confidence of labour, beyond any question or doubt it should be left to the heads of these labour organizations to suggest to the government who in their opinion would be the right man to fill the position. If a system such as this were adopted I believe you would not have the trouble you are having with labour to-day. It is impossible for a man who has not had actual connection with labour to understand the problems of labour. If you have such men in the Department of Labour to advise the department you will have much less trouble than you are having at present.
I am, as I say, in complete agreement with this resolution, and I wish it distinctly understood that I am not saying anything whatsoever against Mr. MacNamara. He is probably as good a man as could be chosen by the department for the position, unless the system were adopted of having the labour men themselves suggest to the government the man to fill the position.

I do not intend to deal fully with all the remarks that have been made, 'because there has been unanimity as to the qualifications of the appointee as associate deputy minister of labour. I understand that the remarks of the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) did not apply to the proposed appointee. I refuse to speculate as to the person against whom he was directing his remarks-
It was perfectly obvious.

-but I would say that since I have been Minister of Labour I have received excellent cooperation from every head of every major labour organization in Canada.
I do not propose to go farther than that.
I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) as to the necessity of strengthening the Department of Labour. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) was kind enough to suggest that he had nothing against the individual appointee, but he thought we were unnecessarily increasing the expenditure in this appointment. I suppose everything is relative, and from my observation I believe it to be true that the Department of Labour has for some considerable time been understaffed and undermanned. Irrespective of the additional work involved in connection with unemployment insurance-the leader of the opposition suggests that that is the duty of a commission, but still the department will have some functions-irrespective of war emergency training; irrespective of the fact that during the war we are carrying the

Industrial Disputes
additional burden of these boards that we are appointing under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, I believe the appointment can be justified outside of the particular war measures. But we are at war.
In connection with the permanency of the appointment something was said about salary. I believe we were peculiarly fortunate in obtaining the services of Doctor Stewart as deputy minister of labour. He has had wide experience. Let me tell the committee something. The salary he is accepting now-and there is no permanency about it; he took it because Canada is at war-the salary he is receiving, with the tax he is paying on it, is only half of the salary he ordinarily receives. In other words it is not a great and generous emolument, but he is doing this work because he is a Canadian and wants to help this country in time of war. I pay that tribute to him.
What will happen after the war is another matter. But certainly I think no member of this committee would suggest that we are not going to have any labour problems after the war. I believe that in the appointment of Mr. MacNamara as associate deputy minister we are making an appointment that will be for the general benefit of this country. I might go farther; but I believe that the appointment is sound. It is made for the reason that I suggested, so that the appointment may be permanent; and I wish to express appreciation in this committee for the almost unanimous support which it has received.

I do not think that there will be any opposition to this resolution on the part of the group with which I am associated. As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) has said, it involves some additional burden upon the taxpayer to foot the bill for highly paid executives. On the other hand, living in such times as these, with the problems faced by a nation fighting in this tremendous war, the function of labour is exceedingly important. While I do not know the specific duties assigned to this new appointment, I will say that if the department can keep labour and management functioning smoothly, the money will be well spent. If there is anything we do not want to happen, it is any retardation of our industrial war effort, the responsibility for which comes upon labour and management alike.
During the course of the debate the postwar effect has been brought into the discussion. Personally I deplore the mention of such things as relief after the war is over. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) referred to the tremendous burden
upon the Department of Labour under the predecessor of the present minister, in connection with the administration of relief, and its activities in the matter of youth training. Let us so manage the affairs of this country now that when the war is over, management and labour will work together to bring about a better country, a more populous country, a country industrialized not only in one part but throughout. Let us not wait until after the war before we do this, because if we have to go through ten years of po^t-war depression we Shall be headed for another war worse than the present one. Let us look forward to a great and glorious Canada after this war has been won.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST

speechtext:
Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of Bill No. 96, to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Vien in the chair.
On section 1-Members not to have pecuniary or other interest.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
The bill at present before the committee is confined to one principle. The present law reads that-
No person shall act as a member of a board who has any pecuniary interest in the issue of a dispute referred to such board.
I do not know how the department interpreted the section as it now stands, but it would, I assume-and it should, I think- debar any party in interest from becoming a member of a board. The suggestion in that regard is to change the law from what I have read to this, that:
No person shall act as a member of a board who has any pecuniary interest, direct or otherwise,-
Which would make it more exclusive.
-in the issue of a dispute referred to such board.
The scope of the prohibition is intended, I think, to be practically all-exclusive. But it goes further and definitely bars anyone who- -has so acted within a period of six months preceding the date of the application for a
Industrial Disputes

board in the capacity of solicitor, legal adviser, counsel or paid agent of either of the parties to the dispute.
If I apprehend aright the minister's proposal in this regard, it is this. The theory of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act is based on the principle of conciliation, which, of course, is very proper. If, as has frequently happened in cases of boards of arbitration, with which I am quite familiar, the interested parties name representatives who in turn agree on an umpire or referee, those interested parties are by the very nature of their employment advocates of the particular ' interest which has appointed them. The judicial aspect is very largely lost sight of.
1 have not had very much experience with conciliation boards, but on one occasion a good many years ago I did act on a board as a representative of one of the interested parties. I was counsel to the party, at the same time. I soon found my position to be almost impossible, because I had to choose between taking dictation from my client, on the one hand, and endeavouring to act independently, and thereby losing my client, on the other. I had to have the thing out, there and then, and assert the principle that a member of a conciliation board was acting in a judicial capacity, and not as an advocate. Therefore I am in accord with the principle that members of the boards of conciliation under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act should be in the position of judicial officers, acting independently, with a primary objective of conciliation, and not of acting as advocates.
I should like to hear anyone who holds a contrary view discuss the other side of the argument, if there be another side. I do not believe this measure is aimed at any particular individual. I have no knowledge of anything of the sort, but I do suggest that the extension of the original principle, namely, that a member of a conciliation board should not be a party either directly or indirectly interested in the result, is a sound one. Whether or not the language of the proposed section is sufficient, I cannot at the moment say. I have not had time to study the drafting of it, but with the underlying principle I can agree. I would commend the minister upon the proposal. It may be that we can improve upon the suggestion made.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I shall not make comment on the legal side of the question, or that part of the measure which refers to legal advisers, counsel or paid agents. But I am wondering who is going to represent the strikers in the event of a dispute. For instance, we will suppose that the steamfitters' union in a city are called out on strike. They do not go
[Mr. R. B. Hanson.l
out unless they are advised by their representatives that they have ample reasons for striking. It may be that they have not come to an agreement with their employers. In my time I have seen quite a number of steamfitters' strikes, because steamfitters' associations were associated with the line of business in which I was engaged. The same would apply to plumbers; I have seen a number of plumbers' strikes, and strikes of machinists. With them, too, I was directly associated. The same observation would apply to moulders; with them, too, I was associated. In fact, in my early days I was engaged in these lines of trade, therefore I have before me the point of view of the worker. On the other hand, I am not opposed to the industrialist, because in due course I became an executive of a large industrial corporation.
I do not believe that the worker goes on strike unless he feels he has some reason for so doing. Conciliation is by far the best course to follow. There should be give and and take on both sides. In the event of a dispute between a machinists' union, or unions of plumbers, moulders or steamfitters, and their employers, and in the further event of the setting up of a board to settle the dispute, I am wondering if paid representatives of the workers would be barred from presenting their case. Who will present the case for them? Certainly the men themselves would be best qualified through their agents to state what their troubles are. Do I understand that under the bill the agent of a steamfitters' union, a machinists' union or a moulders' union, because he is a paid agent of such union, is barred from appearing before the board?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: No.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: If so, who will present the case for the workers?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: The hon. member for Davenport has mentioned cases where men may be out on strike. If they are doing war work, and go out on strike before a board is appointed, they are striking illegally. But the provisions of this amendment do not apply to those who will present the case. As the leader of the opposition has pointed out, this is designed against anyone sitting on the board who may be partially inclined. In other words, the agent of the steamfitters' union or any other union may present his case to the board. The only limitation prescribed in the amendment is that, if they are paid agents, they shall not sit on the board.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
The bill presented by the minister, as I read it, seeks to bring about

Industrial Disputes
impartiality in the men comprising the personnel of a board. Reading the bill, however, as it is now worded, I take the view which has been indicated by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). I do not know where the minister would find men of that mind. In fact, I view this bill in very much the same light as I viewed a story I heard which concerned two Irishmen who were discussing the question of neutrality. The first Irishman wanted to know where his friend, from the south, stood in reference to the war. "Well," was the reply, "I am neutral." "Yes," said the first Irishman, "I can well understand that you are neutral, but who are you neutral for?" That is just about the situation we would have if this bill were passed in its present form.
In my view this is not the proper approach to the problem. Many other things are necessary to clarify the present situation so far as labour is concerned. This' measure would apply to men who are handling cases for labour before conciliation boards. Officials of unions are not allowed to sit on boards, nor are the paid agents of the operators. There are a few lawyers in Canada who have specialized in labour legislation and who, in connection with labour disputes, have made themselves the servants of labour. If this bill were to pass in its present form it would mean that labour's side of the case would not be represented on boards. Only a few of the men to whom I have referred have specialized in labour law. If this bill goes through practically everyone who is connected with labour or who has made a specialty of labour problems will be excluded. You will have full representation of the management and you will have a board with that point of view. You will not have an impartial board, or one that will take an unbiased view of the problems with which the department may be faced. The Department of Labour must recognize the problems that it has to contend with, and an attempt must be made to cure them. There is no use trying to treat the effect; you must treat the cause if you are to have any satisfactory adjustment of the labour situation in Canada at the present time.
I have been connected with organized labour for the past thirty years. I have seen these disputes developing and I have seen partial cures effected. I feel quite sure that the solution to this problem lies in organization. Giving the workers the right to organize is the key to the whole situation. Where the workers are organized in an industry, committees are appointed which meet with the management; collective agreements are signed which set out wages and working conditions;
the operators meet with the men and understand their problems, while the men gain a fairly good idea of the problems faced by the management. It is often found that disputes arise where the workers are unorganized. The government should live up to its own regulations and attempt to allay the unrest which is developing. I do not care what the personnel of this board is to be, it will not be able to cure this situation.
We are supposed to be fighting a war for democracy, a war to overcome Hitler. Spokesmen for the government have emphasized the fact that Hitler destroyed the trade unions of that country and therefore the workers of this country should be ready to give their all for victory. With that we agree wholeheartedly. I think Sir Walter Citrine expressed this very well. His remarks are. quoted in' the Canadian Congress Journal of December 1940. Here is what he said:
Trade unionism is both a cause and a product of democracy. It can only function in an atmosphere of free expression. It cannot function in cellars or behind closed doors. It must impress the public mind, and it must be given facilities to do that. Trade unionism basically is the assertion of the rights of the common man, of the principle that it is not ordained by God that any community should be ruled by aristocracies, whether those aristocracies are of birth or wealth. In pursuit of that principle of voluntary organization, you will find that organizations and groups of people have developed in every corner of the land, meeting to promote some laudable purpose.
That statement is followed up in the January 1941 issue.

I believe the minister has only good intentions, but I feel sure that this bill will make a condition that is already bad, much worse. The minister would be well advised to withdraw the bill and give the whole matter further consideration. The proper approach to the problem is by way of consultation with the men.

Mr. McLarty moves
that the rule be suspended and that the hon. gentlemen have leave to speak to the point.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: While in a sense I have no objection to the suspension of the rule, its suspension might be unduly restricted. It might be suspended to allow the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) to speak, and that might be the end of it, with objection raised by the chair to other hon. members being allowed to speak. Under the circumstances, since we have allowed the second reading to pass without saying what we wanted to say, I think we shall have to leave it now until the third reading.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: May I ask if the bill prohibits any counsel or agent being appointed to a board who in the previous six months represented any association or industry which was one of the parties in a dispute? All the unions have paid agents who are most familiar with their particular problems, but as I understand this amendment the paid agents of the unions, men who have been chosen by the unions for their ability to present their case, will be barred from appointment to the board if they have so acted within a period of six months preceding. The same applies to counsel. I know different counsel who are thoroughly familiar with disputes of this kind, and under this amendment they will be barred if within the six months preceding they have appeared in the capacity of counsel for either of the parties to the dispute. I know a prominent counsel for labour, Mr. Bernard Rose, K.C., of Montreal, perhaps one of the best posted on labour disputes of any counsel I know, and if he has acted for any labour organization during the preceding six months he could not be named to the board. I mention his name only as one I know of; there may be many others. What I say would apply to all counsel who in the preceding six months had presented to a board the case of some union or industry for which he acted. Under this provision I am afraid that quite a large number of counsel and a number of paid union agents will be barred from appointment to a board. Yet the minister, I know, wants to have on these boards the most capable men he can find.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I think perhaps the hon. member for Davenport is not making the distinction that applies, at least in my own mind, in this case. He mentions the name of Mr. Bernard Rose of Montreal, a very estimable man, by way of example. There is no reason

Industrial Disputes
why he cannot present a case before a board, and probably, because of his particular qualifications, why he should not sit on a board. Anyone can present a case subject to section 42 of the act. The original intent of the act was to devoid it, so far as possible, of all legal technicalities. Counsel would appear only in the event of unanimous consent on *the part of the board. The legal restriction which this amendment imposes is not on the presentation of a particular case by labour on the one hand or by industry on the other. It is merely a question of who shall constitute the board, and, as the leader of the opposition has suggested, the whole purpose is to secure a board in which there will not be advocates of one side and advocates of another. The reason for that I think is obvious.
Incidentally this proposed legislation has secured the approval of the national labour supply council, on which both labour and industry are represented. The purpose of the amendment is to secure so far as possible more unanimous reports from a board. It was pointed out to me that in one case one of the members of the board prepared the brief for one of the parties appearing before it, and if you get that definite advocacy it is pretty nearly impossible to get a unanimous report. It is with a view to endeavouring to secure more unanimity in the board's reports that this legislation is introduced.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: I do not think the minister quite caught my point. This amendment imposes a restriction and would bar a very large number of capable counsel and agents of labour organizations from being appointed to a board. I have no doubt that a counsel or labour agent, once he is appointed to a board, would very quickly assume the impartiality of an arbitrator or judge and try to be fair. But this six months' limitation would bar from appointment to the board a considerable number of men who would be well qualified to exercise good judgment in these disputes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member is giving it too wide an application. It means that those who have acted within six months preceding for a particular company-not other companies in general-or for a particular union-not unions in general-would be debarred from membership on a board that was hearing a dispute in which that company or union appeared. He would be qualified to act with respect to other companies or unions.

The minister said that the national labour supply council had given its approval to this bill. Has this council its
full personnel at the present time? If it has given its approval, is that really not approval by only a partial membership of the board?

speechtext: I think the board is full. The hon. gentleman will have to be more specific. I have a letter signed either by the chairman or the secretary of the national labour supply council stating that this measure has its approval.

I have it from one of the members who was on the board at the beginning and the minister says he is still on the board, that so far from approving this bill he is opposed to it.
