maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Would the hon. member for Vancouver East allow me the privilege of dealing very briefly with a remark he made before the committee took recess? It was in connection with the recommendation of the national labour supply council. In the intervening time I have had an opportunity of taking it up with the secretary of the council, and he advises me that there was no recorded opposition to the resolution approving this proposed- legislation.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
In saying a few words on this section I wish to assure the minister that it is my desire to be helpful. Since he has had the honour of holding his present office I have tried on every possible occasion to assist him in this house, so much so that on one occasion I was accused by some of his followers of looking for some preferment. However, I forgave them. I have even tried to help the minister outside the house, so far as I could do so with propriety. I wish to offer him some advice now, and I think he would be wise to accept it.
It is strange that this act, which stands so much in need of overhauling, should be amended at this time only to the extent of this one section. I do not think there is a more dangerous section for him to amend, particularly in the way he is now asking parliament to amend it. The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act was passed in 1907, and for thirty-four years this section has stood the test. So far as I know, there has never been any objection to it until now. Why is there objection now? If I were to take the time of the committee at this stage to tell why, I rather think the chairman would stop me, and perhaps rightly. On some other occasion I will discuss the matter from that point of view. Let me read the old section 12:
Industrial Disputes

No person shall act as a member of a board who has any direct pecuniary interest in the issue of .a dispute referred to such board.
This is direct and simple. We know what it means. It means that no one connected with the management on one side or, on the other side, with the employees who would stand to gain or lose by a decision in the dispute, can be a member of a board. The amendment departs from that simple, direct stipulation. Let me read the section as amended:
No person shall act as a member of a board who has any pecuniary interest, direct or otherwise, in the issue of a dispute referred to such board or who is then acting or has so acted within a period of six months preceding the date of the application for a board in the capacity of solicitor, legal adviser, counsel or paid agent of either of the parties to the dispute.
Let us take the first word that is new- direct or "otherwise". What does "otherwise" mean? Who could not be excluded by the word "otherwise"? Every member of society to-day has a pecuniary interest in almost any labour dispute. Suppose there is a labour dispute in a public utility providing light, heat and power or perhaps transportation. If an increase in wages would affect the rates, or if an increase in wages were denied, rates not being affected, then every member in that community would be affected by the dispute because he would have an interest either direct or "otherwise". So that when you use this word you do not know what it means, or whom it excludes.
Take the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman), who so valiantly protects capital here. If he has shares in a company no one knows whether he has those shares or not. How do you find out? Having a pecuniary interest, he may be affected indirectly in the dispute.
In this amendment the minister is going into a field the limits of which neither he nor anyone else can define. However, I am not sure that that is what the amendment really contemplates. In my opinion it is directed at the representatives of labour who appear on these boards.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: And industry.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
No, because industry has the same representatives on these boards as it has always had. Quite recently, however, certain solicitors have specialized in this kind of work, and I am satisfied that it is at these the amendment is directed, and it is at these that it will be directed. That is why it is so dangerous, particularly at this time. Take a paid agent. To whom does that apply? Where does it get us? I am a member of the amalgamated association of
(Mr. Maclnnis.]
street railway employees in Vancouver. A paid agent of a local of some organization, say in Toronto or Regina or Calgary, would be prevented by this proposal from sitting on a board for the employees of the street railway men in Vancouver, though he would not be directly affected by any decision that might be made in the dispute.
I suggest to the minister in all earnestness that he should consider the matter carefully before pressing this amendment as it stands. It was never intended that a board under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act should be impartial. It has always been impossible to have an impartial board, and it will still be impossible after this amendment is passed. Every member sitting on the board has an opinion one way or another. He is prejudiced, no matter how much or how little, in favour of one side or the other. We try to get over that by getting a judge as chairman-not always, but quite often. While a judge is not necessarily more impartial than some one else, yet because of his position and his training in weighing evidence, he may as chairman of such a board take perhaps a more impartial attitude than the ordinary business or professional man.
Let me read from thp act how the board is set Up:
9. For the purposes of appointment of the members of the board, the following provisions shall apply:

(a) each party to the dispute may, at the time of making application or within five days after being requested so to do by the minister, recommend the name of one person who is willing and -ready to act as a member of the board, and the minister shall appoint such person a member of the board.
Now, what happens? The employees will select a man who, they consider, has the viewpoint and the interest of the employees or workers. The employers, on the other hand, will select a man who has the interest of the employers and the point of view of employers. No matter how you deal with it you are not going to get a more impartial board than you had before.
Then we come to the appointment of the chairman. The minister, after the appointment of the other two members, instructs them to get together and select a chairman. If they fail to do so, the minister appoints the chairman. Usually, and I think for very good reasons, the minister appoints a supreme court judge or some other high court judge. Generally speaking I believe the minister's appointments give satisfaction. They give satisfaction that would not be given if someone other than a judge were appointed.
Yesterday in introducing the bill the minister said that the purpose was to get a more

Industrial Disputes
impartial board. You cannot get a more impartial board, because in spite of what you do the employees will select a person who favours their position, and the employers will select a person who favours their's. You are then as you were'-but with this difference, with this amendment the workers will be limited to a very small number of trained people from whom they can select, while the employers will not be limited at all. There are dozens of corporation lawyers in Canada who are well able to present the case for the employers, but the lawyers who are able to present the case for labour are very few, because labour is not able to afford high-priced lawyers. If this amendment is passed it will prevent labour from taking advantage of any wide choice, and instead of bettering the situation the minister is going to have trouble which I am sure he does not contemplate at the present time.
I said I was going to offer advice to the minister, and I do so with the greatest sincerity. My advice to him is to withdraw the bill.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I am sure the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) are sincerely intended and well meant, and deserve a reply. In the first place I should like to clear up a statement which he apparently believes to be correct but which is not correct, that this amendment is directed at certain particular counsel who are acting for labour. I could give him a number of illustrations that I think would reveal to him that the whole purpose and function of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act was being thwarted by corporation counsel, counsel acting for corporations, who sat on boards. He points out quite truly that although the act was introduced in 1907 it is being used in a very much wider field and given a wider application by reason of its extension on November 7, 1939, to all war industries.
The hon. member said it will be impossible to get a man who is perfectly impartial. Probably I must agree with that. But if representations are to be made to a board I suggest they can be made by representatives before a board, and let us try to make that board as impartial as we possibly can. That is the whole purpose of this amendment. There is no change in the right of representation of either labour or industry before a board. But let me ask this committee this question:	How are you going to get a
unanimous report from any board where the representative on the one hand is counsel for a corporation and the representative on the other hand is counsel for a labour body?
I am not oblivious to the fact that it will be difficult to get complete impartiality. The amendment cannot guarantee that. But what it can do is it can take a step toward securing that impartiality. There will have to be, of course, some definite application to determine the mode of procedure which will be adopted to ensure impartiality. But I believe this is a step in the right direction. While it does not guarantee that every board will be impartial, at least it is a move in that direction, and for that reason I think should commend itself to the committee.
As the hon. member has stated, in cases where the power of appointment has fallen to me I have generally appointed a judge. There are two reasons for so doing. First, it is some assurance of impartiality; at least you are not open to any suggestion that you are trying to be partial to either side. And second, a judge should be most competent to weigh, consider and adjudicate upon the evidence given.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I agree with the principle of this bill, but I believe a great deal of difficulty will be involved in the way it will work out. In the first place it will be found that both sides will be devoting considerable time to investigating the representative of the other side to be sure that he is not either directly or indirectly interested in the dispute. As the minister has pointed out, both sides will have the opportunity of being represented at the hearing by their solicitor or representative, whichever they prefer. It has been the practice of labour organizations down through the years to have, if possible, their paid agents, men who have been following the case, arguing the case and debating it with these various boards. They know that these men have at heart the interests of the people they represent and have a definite knowledge of the problems to be debated, and in that respect will be in the best position to put forward the claims of the people who are before the board.
In the three or four years that this act has been in effect there have been at different times many complaints; in fact, if my memory serves me aright, not long ago there was quite a discussion over the fact that the chairman of a board was found to have a direct interest in a dispute which was under investigation. But I understand that the various ministers of labour have had a list of men across Canada who it is considered would be suitable chairmen of the various boards. While there have been mistakes in the past in the selection of chairmen, on the whole the system has worked out very satisfactorily. In the vast

Industrial Disputes

majority of cases impartial decisions have been rendered by the chairmen on the evidence as it was placed before them. I am sure that every hon. member wishes to see these cases decided as impartially as it is possible to decide them. As one of the previous speakers stated, it is impossible to find any person who is entirely impartial, but so long as we can find people who are willing to be fair to both points of view, that is about all we can expect from the normal human being.
Again I must say that I agree with and approve heartily the principle of the bill; nevertheless I have grave doubts as to its success in actual practice.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
The principle of appointing arbitrators and the constitution of the board as embodied in the bill are copied from the arbitration acts of the various provinces. In some cases, it is true, members of boards do not know very much about the work. When labour saw fit to nominate a member of the board, the principle was adopted of having each party to a dispute nominate a member, and the chairman of the board was chosen by agreement, failing which the Minister of Labour made the appointment. On some occasions it has been difficult to obtain a labour man to act without remuneration. When I speak of labour men I have not in mind the agitator type. I have had a great deal to do with the appointment of some of these boards, and it has not always been easy to get a labour man to act unless he could be assured of some compensation. I am not speaking of the sort of labour man who goes around stirring up strife. That sort of thing is bad enough in our industrial life in time of peace; it is far worse in war time.
I should not like to see the minister, unless he finds it necessary as a war measure, keep off the boards some of our reasonable, bona fide labour men who have given a great deal of help to the trade union movement in this country. Not a few disputes have arisen with respect to public utilities connected with the municipalities, operating at cost. In such cases they generally secured pretty good boards, nominated by each side. In some cases the minister chose the chairman, in others the senior judge of the county was appointed. However, with due respect to the bench, a number of the judges who have functioned on these commissions knew very little about the practical matters connected with mechanization which arise in the very involved industrial disputes of the present day. But let me repeat, from my observation, the minister has chosen very good men to act on these boards.

I do not agree with the practice of some members of the legal profession going all over the country to participate in every petty dispute which arises here, there and everywhere. Although I am a member of the legal profession, I have not a great deal of sympathy with that type of professional man. There are some good men among them, but I know others who are not in favour of the thorough prosecution of this war, and after all, industrial disputes-as is evident from the experience of the United States-will be a menace to the war effort unless the government lays down some policy with respect to such issues when they arise. We are now away behind with our war effort, and there is not a day to be lost.
Some time ago in the case of Snyder vs the Toronto Electric commission, I was associated with an appeal to the privy council to determine whether sections of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act were intra vires of the parliament of Canada in regard to public utilities as certain sections of that act of that day were involved in a labour dispute with the system's, employees; and after all Canadian courts it came before decided it was, the privy council gave a very important judgment on the matter of property and civil rights in the province, the law of contracts and that of employers and employees. The late Lord Haldane delivered the judgment of the court, which was a very good one, and dealt with the constitution of the board and the duties of its members.
I have been all my life a supporter of labour, especially the trade union movement. When properly administered, without the intrusion of agitators, it has been in many ways a blessing to this country. In my opinion some good labour men can be engaged as members of boards, but they cannot afford to lay off w'ork without remuneration for one, two or three months. I know of one involved arbitration which lasted fifteen months. It arose out of the taking over of the street railway by the city of Toronto, and cost nearly a million and a half dollars.
I am sorry that I was not in the chamber this morning. Has the minister any information from the old country as to a change, under war-time conditions, in the constitution of the British boards? Is it now the law of England that they are not to be paid?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Not as far as I know.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
County court judges receive. I believe, $25 a day. They are allowed by the tariff $15 a day, but when they relinquish their other judicial duties it is our practice to give them $25 a day and expenses.

Industrial Disputes
As 1 have said, there are some very good labour men. I might mention Mr. Joseph Gibbons, who has served on one or two commissions. I am sorry that his services are not more frequently utilized.
I will support this measure if the government thinks it is necessary in connection with the war effort, although it seems to me rather dangerous to upset in times of war an arrangement which has worked well in times of peace.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: There is one matter mentioned by the hon. member for Broadview as to which I might make a correction. Nothing in this bill prevents any labour man or any representative of industry from receiving the fees prescribed by the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. In other words, the mere fact that he is a member of the board will not constitute him a counsel or paid agent of either employer or employee. The fees may not be very large, but we have had no difficulty in finding people to serve for them. Consequently labour will not be in a prejudicial position in that regard.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I rose to ask the minister a question a few moments ago. I understood him to say that certain regulations would be made as a result of this amendment. Those regulations, I suppose, will specify just what classification a man will come under who has some pecuniary interest in a dispute. Not only will the Department of Labour get into more and more difficulty as a result of this amendment but, as was suggested by the hon. members for Vancouver East and Davenport, I believe the government is taking away the type of arbitration board formerly intended. It is taking away from labour some of the rights they formerly enjoyed.
It is not always that a question of wages is involved. Sometimes questions of working conditions have to be considered. A dozen and one different questions may be involved in a labour dispute, questions which have nothing whatever to do with wages. Therefore in order to have its case properly placed before other members of the board, it is necessary that labour have someone there who has a practical knowledge of the situation.
The minister has pointed out that labour may submit evidence to the board. But, in choosing the member of a board, labour is not going out to choose one who is not conversant with labour conditions. The attitude of labour on various questions has been one of desire and hope of bettering their conditions. How far-reaching, then, is this amendment going to be? If a person is a member of a trade union, a member of a trade congress or of the Canadian congress of labour, and 14873-228}
a matter of vital importance to the whole set-up of unions in Canada is involved, that person would have a pecuniary interest and would be debarred. In any matter which is going to benefit his union, even though it may be a dispute with another union, he is bound to have a pecuniary interest.
The minister is the one who will have to say whether or not a man has that interest. Should the minister refuse to accept a nominee of labour on the ground that he may have some interest, the minister would be in very serious difficulty, and would immediately have all the labour organizations in the country on his neck.
I feel very much as did the hon. members for Vancouver East and Davenport. I do not see how we can gain anything from this amendment, and I feel that we are going to have more difficulties in the Department of Labour in designating who is or who is not interested. If the minister is anxious to have a non-partisan board to deal with labour disputes, a board before which labour and industry, and whoever else may be involved, may state their positions, then rather than curb the type of representation one can have on the board, I suggest that labour and all other parties concerned would be much better off if the minister would say, "We will appoint a board of judges in every province who will sit on these disputes, and to which evidence may be submitted under oath." This bill is unfair to labour; under its provisions labour is the group whose representations will be curbed.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
At first glance I did not see anything objectionable in the bill, but after hearing the hon. member for Vancouver East I have somewhat altered my opinion. I did not hear everything he said, but I gathered from what I did hear that he was voicing the opinions of labour unionism, and stating their opposition to this bill. He may not have had direct authority-and I do not see how he could have had, because the bill was introduced only a few hours ago-to speak for labour. But if any hon. members can lay claim to representing labour, then I should think the hon. member for Vancouver East must be one of them. So far as I can gather he appears to make strong objection to this bill.
The very essence of the bill, as in respect to similar legislation, appears to me to be framed on cooperation, on the getting together of labour and capital, in order to come to some reasonable arrangement. Any suggestion of doing so by way of legislation which has the appearance of having been forced on one or other of these bodies would be bound to react unfavourably against any prospects of cooperation in any dispute.
Industrial Disputes

As it has been opposed-and it has been strongly opposed-by people representing labour, I suggest that we might accept the suggestion offered by the hon. member for Vancouver East, namely, that of withdrawing the bill; or it might be stood over until the next session. It is rumoured that we will meet in a couple of months-not likely more than three months. By that time publicity will be given to the purpose of the amendment, and it would be possible to have a better idea as to the way in which it would be accepted by labour.
There is one other point I would mention to the minister. In the bill we find the expression "No person . . . who has any pecuniary interest, direct or otherwise". It might be possible in high places-and I do not at all suggest that it could happen under the present minister-that under some circumstances there might come a time when it would be desirable to favour one party's interests rather than those of another. It would be possible for whoever had the deciding of the issue to regard the recommendation of the labour group as undesirable. That group might select, we will say, Tom>
Jones, a prominent labour sympathizer, but a person not essentially connected with the dispute. It might be possible to say, "No, we will not accept that man, because he has an 'otherwise' interest." In other words he may have an indirect interest in the dispute.
We will suppose that it would be a dispute between the employees and the management of a street railway company. It would be possible to refuse the appointment of a man not directly connected with labour, but one who is perhaps known to be a sympathizer. The argument might be used that as he was a potential passenger on the street car it would be possible, if the demands of the labour element were accepted, that the price of street car tickets would be increased. Therefore it would always be possible to turn down nominee after nominee until a man was secured who was more or less favourable to the other side of the argument. It is going too far to prevent a man from acting as a representative in a dispute because he might have an "otherwise", in other words an indirect, interest in such dispute.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
In connection with this matter I believe I fall in line with the observations of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). At first I did not see very much that was wrong in the bill, and I thought the word "otherwise" might tend to make the conciliation board more impartial. I believe now, however, that it will deprive labour of its chance of being represented by people who in other ways might not be objectionable.

I suggest that what the government ought to do is to stop strikes before they start. Do not let them get started. Do not let us have any of these stoppages in war work. The government should do everything possible to see that such stoppages are prevented. There must be no suspicion of injustice in the minds of the people of Canada, and particularly in the minds of labour. I believe if the word "otherwise" is left in the bill it will be just one more small thing which might cause a good deal of trouble. It would develop suspicion, and thereby render it more difficult to prevent stoppages of work.
We must remember that a great many people in Canada, and practically all people in Great Britain, have given up many privileges. We are going to have those privileges back after the war; in the meantime I think we are all satisfied to be deprived of them. In my opinion the government should make it very clear that in the matter of dealing with labour disputes there will be no injustice, and that they are not going to take a dictatorial attitude on behalf either of labour or of capital in connection with war work in Canada. In other words the government must take a firm stand. The very fact of having the word "otherwise" in the bill will mean that there will be suspicion, and just another small cause for discontent with the board. I believe the minister would be wise in removing that word and thereby removing suspicion.
Mr. O'NEILL:	I have listened with a
great deal of interest to the argument that has been put forward on this bill. I am not always in agreement with the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), nor am I always in agreement with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I have been directly connected with labour for thirty-five years, but I have not been delegated to speak for labour at this time. I believe the minister is sincerely trying to make these boards of conciliation more impartial, but I am in agreement with the hon. member for Vancouver East when he says that that is almost impossible. As the hon. member said, labour will appoint a man who has the labour viewpoint, and the employer will appoint a man with the employer viewpoint. This bill will restrict the field from which labour can draw. Right now we have a board of conciliation and it may be necessary in three months' time to have another board. Will this legislation not prevent either capital or labour from continuing to have as their representatives the men who are now sitting on the board?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
That is not the intention.

Industrial Disputes
Mr. O'NEILL: It says "counsel or paid agent."

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
They would receive their pay under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act and would not come within the purview of this amendment.
Mr. O'NEILL:	I am glad to have that
explanation, but the language of this bill may be construed differently to-morrow by a lawyer. It is not what the minister's opinion may be, it is the interpretation that will be placed upon the law. With all due respect to the minister, I must say I am afraid that this bill will prove detrimental to labour, and I suggest that he withdraw it at this time.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
Perhaps I could say a few
words as one who has been watching the situation for a considerable length of time. We have had boards which were quite successful in settling disputes to the satisfaction of all concerned, and Which brought down findings which had a fairly binding effect. We have had other boards which reached divided decisions and where it was found that the settlements arrived at were temporary indeed. The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act provides for the setting up of what is in effect a judicial board, but recently a practice has crept in under which you have practically a board of arbitration. One side appoints an agent to represent it, the other side appoints another agent to represent it, and the Department of Labour appoints a judge or someone else as the third and only neutral member of the board. The findings rendered by many of these boards have not been beneficial to the settlement of disputes.
Perhaps we could take a specific case which has been referred to quite often in this house, the Peck rolling mills dispute. In that case an agent of the union was appointed as a member of the board along with the paid solicitor of the Peck rolling mills. A member of the judiciary was the third member. I suggest that that was not a conciliation board. In my opinion such a board could never agree. If the paid representative of the union and the representative of the employer could agree, the board would not have been necessary. The Minister of Labour is attempting to set up a tribunal which will assess the facts submitted to it and attempt to arrive at a mutual agreement based upon the facts presented by the two sides.
The government has no intention of barring the representatives of either side from appearing before the board. The representative of the union is entitled to appear and state his case as ably as he possibly can. Similarly,
the company may send its paid solicitor before the board to represent the case for the company. But after that has been done, a decision is rendered by three men who have open minds on the subject. One man would have the view of labour, because we would assume that labour would choose a man who held such views. Another man would have the view of the owner, because we would assume that the company would choose a man of that type. Then we know that the Minister of Labour would choose a man with a judicial mind, one without any particular views on either side. We believe that that would be a board which would reconcile the facts brought before it and bring down a finding which both sides could accept as a reasonable settlement of the dispute.
Hon. gentlemen know that the success of the Department of Munitions and Supply depends almost entirely on the continuance of good relations between capital and labour. The highest objective I have in conducting the department is that those relations shall obtain. I discussed this matter with several labour leaders representing different occupational groups and I did not hear one dissenting voice to my suggestion that a completely impartial board of three would be more effective in solving labour disputes than the practice that has lately cropped up of appointing special advocates and special pleaders for each party with only one neutral arbitrator.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I quite agree with what
the Minister of Munitions and Supply has said, but to my mind it does not clear the situation. He has said that labour will name someone who is partial to labour and that industry will name someone partial to industry, while the Department of Labour will name the third member. Such a man may not be a pi-ofessional or legal advocate of labour, but he will be a man possessing labour's viewpoint. When sitting on the board he is going to fight for the people who have named him to the board. If we could get what the Minister of Munitions and Supply has suggested we might get it would be a perfect set-up, but I do not think this bill is going to do it. In fact I think this bill is going to make things more difficult for the Department of Labour. I would far rather have the Department of Labour say that impartial boards are to be set up in Ontario and the other provinces to deal with these matters. The time has come when the Department of Labour must show courage in handling a situation of this kind, not only courage in handling labour, but courage in handling the industrial end. We dare not allow either industry or labour to interfere with our war effort. So far there has been too much of it.
Industrial Disputes

The Department of Labour in bringing in this amendment is just bringing upon itself more difficulties. It is giving itself the responsibility of saying to one side or the other in a dispute: We cannot accept your nominee because he has some pecuniary interest in this dispute. If you deny the right to labour to choose its own representative, labour is going to say that you are unfair, and if you deny that right to industry, industry is going to say the same. Yet labour will be the greatest loser.
The minister would be well advised to withdraw this bill and to make up his mind that the Department of Labour will handle these disputes with only one end in view. Being fair, yes, but seeing that nothing shall interfere with the production of the essential raw materials required by this country. There could very well be set up in every province an impartial board, even to the extent of appointing to these boards judges who will sit and hear all disputes between labour and industry. It is a big job, and I sympathize with the minister because I know some of the responsibility that is his. It is a job that has to be handled with courage and yet with great diplomacy. I do think that the minister could work out some better way of dealing with these disputes than the method this bill provides.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: I should like to say a word in reply to the remarks of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. He would be right and I could agree with him if all these disputes were disputes involving wages and conditions. His conclusion was based on the assumption that labour has bargaining powers with the employer, because he said that if an agreement could be arrived at by a board as constituted at the present time, the same understanding could have been arrived at between the employer and the employee.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, w'hat I said was that if the appointees, the paid representative of the labour union and the paid representative of the employer, could ever hope to agree, a board would not have been necessary in the first place. When you add a third party, you get a decision of the board which is a majority decision. But the chance of getting a unanimous decision of the board, where you have a paid representative of one party and a paid representative of the other, is very unlikely unless the employer and the union could have arrived at such an agreement without the intervention of the board.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
In any case, and under any arrangements, you will have a paid repre-

sentative of the employer and a paid representative of the employees, because I presume none of these people is going to work for nothing.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: But paid by the crown.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Paid under the act.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
In those circumstances the employer would be represented 100 per cent. That is my honest conviction.
I may have an opportunity later to express what I had in mind earlier when I was ruled out of order, with respect to a proper solution of the problem. I am convinced that the employer and the employee can iron out their difficulties without boards of conciliation, provided that some of the legal barriers set up by order in council are removed so as to give labour and industry an opportunity of coming together and having their own tribunals through the medium of organization. I think the Minister of Labour will agree that at least 85 per cent of the disputes that have arisen since the outbreak of the war have not been over wages and working conditions but rather over the demand by the employees of recognition of their right to set up a collective bargaining agency. In addition to that phase of the question, which must be thoroughly examined if we are desirous of arriving at a solution, we must remember that the final decision of the board, after it has been set up and has taken evidence from employer and employee, is made as a result of examination of that evidence. If the representative of labour on the board is not qualified, has not the technical training which will enable him to make an examination of the evidence so that a proper report can be brought in with due regard to the people he represents, you are not going to have any solution of the problem.
I will not say any more just now, except that I think the Minister of Munitions and Supply was labouring under a misapprehension, or else I misunderstood him. I feel that he would be right in his contention if labour was organized. I believe that 75 per cent of the boards which have been set up and 75 per cent of the money that is being wasted on them could be eliminated, and then we could get down to business.
Mr. O'NEILL: In my experience I can recall only one conciliation board in a period of thirty-five years which brought in a unanimous report. If that is so, it seems to me that the men who comprise these conciliation boards must be pretty well biased, if I may put it in that way, when they go in there to sit on a board. The representative

Industrial Disputes
of labour will have the labour class viewpoint, and that viewpoint only. He is there for that very reason. Similarly with the man who goes in there to represent the employer; he is there because he has the employer's viewpoint on the subject. I can recall only one case, I say, in thirty-five years where a board brought in a unanimous decision.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
Was that a railwaymen's case?
Mr. O'NEILL: The case I refer to was not
in connection with operating railway men.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. McKinnon) stated a few minutes ago that if this bill carries it will be possible for either party to be represented at the hearing by its counsel or solicitor even * if he had been occupied as counsel for the party within the preceding six months. From my recollection of the act that statement is not correct. Counsel or solicitors may appear for either party at a hearing under this act only by consent of the parties, and even in cases where such consent is given it is still within the power of the board to refuse to allow counsel or solicitors to appear at a hearing. I think that is the provision, and in order to meet the case my hon. friend has in mind, it might be necessary to amend one or two other sections of the act to make it perfectly clear that if the bill carries in its present form counsel would have the right to appear at the call of the party whom they represent.
There is no doubt that the principle as stated by the leader of the opposition this morning is the one which should be applicable to judicial bodies, and if possible to boards of this kind. However, the board set up under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act is not a judicial body. It is a conciliation and investigation board. During the many years in which the act has been administered it has, I know, been the practice for parties to the dispute to cover a very wide range in the selection of the men who are to represent them on the board. There is high authority for the statement that no man can serve two masters. At first blush, it might be said that a solicitor who within a short period prior to a hearing had been representing one of the parties could be regarded as holding a brief for that party, but I suggest that it has not always worked out in that way. Obviously, too, in the setting up of a board of this kind, the parties to the dispute will select their own representatives, and those representatives will reflect the general views of the respective parties. It is not possible in the circumstances to set up a board that could be wholly free from the charge of partiality, or so long
as both parties have the right to choose their own representatives. The amendment reads:
No person shall act as a member of a board who has any pecuniary interest, direct or otherwise, in the issue of a dispute referred to such board or who is then acting or has so acted within a period of six months preceding the date of the application for a board in the capacity of solicitor, legal adviser, counsel or paid agent of either of the parties to the dispute.
If this goes through it will be quite permissible in the case mentioned by the minister or in any similar case to have one of the representatives proposed by the employees turned down on the ground that he had some interest, direct or otherwise, in the subject matter of the dispute, while another person appointed for the employers might be counsel not for one of the parties but for a corporation controlling shares belonging to such party if it happened to be an incorporated company. If one wanted to exhaust all possible anomalies that might arise in dealing with the question of indirect interest one would have to frame a much wider section than this. I am not sure whether it is intended that this legislation should be retroactive or at least whether it is to come into effect at once and be applicable to boards now in existence, but if it is I see no reason why the effect of it might not be to disqualify in some particular case a member of an existing board.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
Will the
minister read the section of the act with regard to the presence of counsel before the boards, and also clarify the words "direct or otherwise"? I have been thinking this over since we were here this morning. Its implications are numerous.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
The section to which the
leader of the opposition refers is section 42 of the act:
No counsel or solicitor shall be entitled to appear or be heard before the board, except with the consent of the parties to the dispute, and notwithstanding such consent the board may decline to allow counsel or solicitors to appear.
With regard to some of the observations that have been made, I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. O'Neill) say that in thirty-five years he had never known of a unanimous board award.
Mr. O'NEILL:	I know of only one.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I can assure him that
during the time I have been Minister of Labour, until recently when this technique has developed, there have been a great many unanimous reports, which were extremely helpful. In fact, I would say that the majority of them were unanimous in the first year, but
Industrial Disputes

this technique has come about and it almost makes it impossible to have unanimous approval because of the interests of either of the parties. I admit frankly that I do not think we shall ever come to the point where we shall have complete impartiality. The fact that a man is appointed either by labour or by industry almost naturally indicates his inclination, and that is all right; but we are not helping to get paid counsel sitting on the boards. This bill was considered by the national labour supply council, on which are the heads of four leading national labour organizations in Canada. They have all approved it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Is Mr. Tom Moore on that?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I do not think there is anything in the bill that would be prejudicial to labour. The suggestion has been made that we are restricting labour. We are not for a moment taking away from labour or industry the right to appoint its member of the board. We are simply saying to labour, as to industry, that there is a very small class that should not be appointed because it would prejudicially affect the impartiality of the board. That is the whole effect of this. Personally I have no objection to deleting the words "direct or otherwise".
Mr. O'NEILL: Let me submit a hypothetical case. Suppose there is an accident just outside the city. A train and an automobile are both racing for the crossing. The automobile is hit, the driver is killed and the engineer is up for manslaughter. Naturally the labour organization will employ the best legal talent they can to protect that man. The case is disposed of, and two months afterwards the engineers become involved with the railway company in a dispute. A conciliation board is appointed. Could the engineers in that case appoint as their representative on the board the lawyer who had defended them in the court action?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I think the answer would be in the negative if he had acted as counsel on behalf of a union within a period of six months.
Mr. O'NEILL: That is the point I am making. You are narrowing the field of those upon whom the labour organizations may. call to act as their agents on a conciliation board.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
The same applies to
industry. The same situation might arise there.	[DOT]
Mr. O'NEILL:	But they have more to
draw from than labour.
[Mr. McLarty.J

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
The bill will be improved slightly by the amendment. I think it will be helpful to the Department of Labour, because they would find it very difficult to define who was or was not affected by having a pecuniary interest in the dispute. But my objection to the section still stands. I am going to propose an amendment that will limit the prohibition not to solicitor, legal adviser, counsel or paid agent who acted for either of the parties, but to one who acted in respect of the dispute then before the board. I therefore move:
That the section be amended by striking out all the words after the word "agent" in the thirteenth line, and that the following be substituted therefor:
"in respect to such dispute or any matter involved therewith."

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: The effect of this proposed amendment would be to eliminate completely the benefit we hope to derive from the general amendment. It means that they may not have been employed as counsel in the particular dispute which is being heard by the board. The purpose of the general amendment is that they shall not have had the pecuniary interest of being employed by a company or of receiving financial remuneration from a union for six months. The hon. member's amendment would simply destroy the effect of the bill, since the limitation would be only in respect to the particular dispute involved. It would render the general amendment useless and prevent us from obtaining what we hope will be an impartial board. Before a dispute arises it is unlikely that there would be consultation with counsel, and the only limitation effected by the amendment of the hon. member would be that they had not been consulted in the particular dispute under review.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: The minister has referred on several occasions to the impartiality of the board, yet I think that both he and the Minister of Munitions and Supply admitted that you could not have an impartial board.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: But should that not be the aim?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
It cannot be the aim
as long as you allow each side to select its representative. It is pure nonsense to talk about an impartial board as long as you say: This man will represent me and that man will represent you and the third man is the umpire. The third man may be impartial or he may not. My own opinion is that he can be impartial only to a certain degree. But counsel may present arguments and help the union or the employees or the employer

Industrial Disputes
to place the evidence before the board. What you are doing with this measure so far as the employees are concerned is limiting them as to the number of qualified experienced persons from whom they can draw who are able to analyse the evidence and stand up against a judge and another trained representative of the employers.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
think that the majority of employees' representatives on boards are as a matter of fact paid by some union in connection with that service?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: No.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: I think not.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
If they are not, why
this section, if it is not aimed at someone? What is the section aimed at if the representative of the employees-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Let me admit that there are some.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Then the purpose of this is to prevent these few or this particular one or two from appearing on boards. The minister should be careful what questions he asks.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: I think it would be fair to my hon. friend if I suggested that more lawyers have been employed by employers appearing on boards than by employees.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Of course, because lawyers do riot work for nothing.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: No one does except members of parliament.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Well, some members of parliament do not work. However, getting back.to the point, the minister withdrew the words "or otherwise" because he found himself .unable to define what they would mean. Can he define the words "of the parties to the dispute"? To whom will they apply? For instance, take my own organization that I mentioned this morning, the amalgamated association of street railway employees in America. If they have as counsel a man who appeared in a case in Toronto for division 113 of the association, would that man be debarred from appointment as representative of division 101 in Vancouver on a similar board? He is possibly a party to the dispute. Does this apply to national organizations, to provincial organizations or to local units?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I do not believe that the amendment would in any wise help, but I do not believe that the bill itself will accomplish what is expected of it. I think we shall find that after passing this bill we shall not have got any nearer to impartiality, for reasons 14873-229
which have been stated by several hon. members. They are simply to this end, that when a person is chosen by either side to the dispute he is chosen because he is a partisan, and we do not change that except to say certain types of partisans may not be chosen. If you cannot have men on the board who are regular counsel or have been regular counsel for the disputants, it seems to me you have to leave it open to the disputants to have their counsel before the board, which sometimes they have and sometimes have not. But I cannot believe that we shall accomplish anything by this legislation. I am in favour of it as it is written, in favour of the idea of getting an impartial board, but in voting for this bill I do not believe we shall really be accomplishing what we are aiming at. It may be well enough to try it for perhaps a year or two, and experience will show whether it has any value or has been a detriment, more particularly in the labour world. Would it not be a good idea, if the bill is passed, to withhold the application of it for a time in order to see what further reactions there may be, more particularly in the labour world, with regard to it? Very often it happens that central labour organizations, such as the advisory body mentioned by the minister, are not thoroughly representative of their membership on the particular issue upon which they are expressing their views. It might be well to hold up the application of the measure for a while.
To sum up, while I shall vote for the legislation, and while I should like to see impartiality achieved, I cannot bring myself to the conviction that we are going to get it as a result of this measure.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
There is one interesting feature of the discussion. I would point out to the minister that hon. members who have opposed this legislation are representative of all three of our groups in the house, and have been intimately associated with labour organization. I refer to the hon. members for Winnipeg South Centre, Kamloops, Kenora-Rainy River, Waterloo South, Cape Breton South, ahd Vancouver East. Under these circumstances it is fairly evident that there is an uneasy feeling among those who are intimately connected with labour organizations and understand the working of these disputes and of the conciliation boards. I believe that feeling will be in the minds of labour at the present time, and if there is one thing all of us should try to avoid, it is giving those elements in our country that are trying to subvert our war effort any opportunity of using anything we do in this house to promote dissatisfaction in the labour field at this time.

Industrial Disputes

I join with others in urging that the bill be withdrawn for the present and that, perhaps, the reaction of organized labour be obtained in order that we may arrive at some conclusion upon the subject.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
Has
organized labour not approved the principle of this bill?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
Oh, yes. So far as
organized labour is concerned, the notification I had from the national labour supply council, which is representative-very representative-of organized labour, was that the matter was unanimously approved, without any recorded dissent in connection with it.
The hon. member for Vancouver East suggested that in agreeing to the withdrawal of the wmrds "direct or otherwise," I did so because I could not explain what it meant. I can assure him that that was not the purpose. I was impressed with the argument that the term might be difficult to apply in the matter of administration, and for that reason I am quite prepared to have it withdrawn.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Would the, minister allow me just one word? I was speaking the day before yesterday to the president of one of the national labour organizations who is or was a member of the national supply board. He told me that he was opposed to this amendment. I did not speak with other representatives of labour here, and consequently I do not know the views of all of them, but that is the position so far as this man is concerned.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: All I can assure this committee of, Mr. Chairman, is that he did not record in any way his dissent from the recommendation that this legislation be passed.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: The minister has stated on two occasions, confirming it in his answer to the hon. member for Vancouver East, that labour as represented on the national labour supply council were unanimous in their approval of this legislation. Is the Canadian congress of labour represented on the supply council at this time?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Yes, they are, but I did not use the word "unanimous" as regards their approval. What I said was that there was no dissent recorded. I took it that the council approved; it was without recorded dissent.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I believe the minister said in reply to the leader of the opposition that the vote was unanimous.
(Mr. Coldwell.l

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: No. Well, I wish to be fair. If I did state that, I was in error. I said that there was no recorded vote to the contrary.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: As a matter of information, may I ask the minister how the provisions of this section will be implemented? How is he going to ensure that the board is impartial within the meaning of this section; and what would be the effect of an award made by the board if it were discovered that one member was not in fact impartial within the meaning of the section?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: That is, perhaps, going pretty far. I suppose that, once the board is established, it will have to be assumed that it is qualified to act, and that a subsequent discovery that the information is wrong should not be allowed to upset the award of the board.	[DOT]

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Probably the minister can clear up a difficulty which has occurred to me. Heretofore, both sides have been appointing their representatives-you can call them legal representatives or agents-on this conciliation board to represent the views of the contending parties. Under section 42 of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, an agent or legal representative is prevented from appearing before the board without the consent of both parties to the dispute. How will employees get their case before this board if they are not allowed to have a solicitor or an agent there to present it?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: There is no prohibition of an agent appearing before the board. Section 42 does not provide that. It says that counsel shall be allowed to appear before the board only with the consent of the board. There is no reason why agents should not be allowed to appear. Of course they will. This will not affect in any way section 42.
