maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I endeavoured to make
a few observations when this measure was before the committee, and I was told that they were not relevant at that time. At this time, therefore, I desire to make a general summary of the measure, as I see it. The bill brought before the house by the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) is one through which ways and means are sought to improve conciliation machinery. In my opinion, however, this bill absolutely restricts and definitely rules out any opportunity labour may have had of having adequate representation on conciliation boards.
I am endeavouring to point out to the minister that the amendment proposed in the bill will serve to make more confusing an already badly confused situation. I believe that the present state of unrest in labour is attributable to at least some of the measures enacted by order in council, but never implemented.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
What
are they?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I refer first to order in
council P.C. 2685, which gives the workers the right to organize. The principle of the right to recognition of trade unions is set out in no uncertain terms right through that order in council. Industry is strongly advised to meet employees, to give them the right to organize, and to sign collective agreements.
Industrial Disputes

That order in council was well worded, but it has never been given legal status. So far as labour in Canada is concerned, order in Council P.C. 2685 is not to-day worth the paper on which it is written. It is advice to those who, in my opinion, are to a great extent responsible for the present situation, but that advice was never followed by action, nor was it given any legal interpretation. The failure of the Department of Labour to follow up that order in council and to see to its enforcement, as the department follows up and sees to the enforcement of legislation which has for its purpose the restriction of the rights of labour in war time, cannot be excused. Practically every piece of legislation in which the rights of labour are restricted has been enforced, but order in council P.C. 26S5 has not been. The bill before the house will only make greater the confusion which at present exists. As I tried to point out this morning, to cure a disease one must get at the cause. The government cannot cure the disease of industrial unrest by operating from the top, through conciliation boards. It must get to the bottom, to the base of the trouble. At the present time that struggle has its basis in the efforts of the workers to form collective organizations through which they may have a say in the management of industry. That is the point from which the government, if it wishes to effect a cure, must work.
The minister must first give some consideration to the enforcement of order in council P.C. 2685. Second, order in council P.C. 7440 was another move which badly confused not only the average workingman but those men who sat in on conciliation boards. They have not been able to interpret it. Perhaps that suggestion is best exemplified in the dispute which has taken place in the rubber industry. The personnel of conciliation boards have not been able to obtain a proper interpretation, or a correct understanding of order in council P.C. 7440, The Minister of Labour will remember that the Bowmanville rubber workers put in motion all the legal machinery of conciliation. A board was set up and made an award of increased wages which was satisfactory to both employer and employees. After that report had been made, the Minister of Labour wrote to the rubber workers' organization in Bowmanville and stated that the conciliation board had erred in its award which had been accepted by employer and employees. It was stated that the decision was over and above what was called for by order in council P.C. 7440, and it was stated that at some future time this organization would be called upon to defer their right to further increases on account of increased costs

of living until such time as the overpayment had been made up. I think in that case the board understood its duties and took the real meaning out of the order in council.
This situation is illustrated by what has occurred at the Peck rolling mill. They put into force all the legal machinery as stipulated by the government. A vote was taken, and an examination of the situation was made. In their Trenton, Nova Scotia, plant, Dominion Iron and Steel pay a base wage of forty-five cents an hour, and the same rate is paid in the Sydney plant. Yet in Quebec they pay only 30-7 cents an hour. The conciliation board split, the majority holding that their interpretation of order in council P.C. 7440 was that the wages paid in 1926 and 1929 should be the basis of the award, and their award was made accordingly. The union representative presented a minority report, which was based upon his interpretation of order in council P.C. 7440, to the effect that in areas where wage levels had been depressed during normal periods, the board had jurisdiction to level up.
As a result of all this, a strike has been in progress in the Peck Rolling Mills for the past month. Employees are suffering, and an organization which should be producing war materials is shut down. Confusion exists because order in council P.C. 7440 beclouds the issue. The interpretation has been given by the Department of Labour that wages must conform to the 1926 and 1929 level irrespective of whether they have been depressed. My information is that not very much is being done to cope with this situation. In my opinion an examination should be made of this entire industry which controls twenty-six subsidiaries from Sydney west into Ontario. The industrial rates of wages should be the same for all plants. If the basic rate in one plant is forty-five cents an hour, then that rate should apply to the entire industry. Instead of this strike being prolonged for a month, instead of the people having to suffer and production being curtailed, the board should have been reinstructed. The wages at the Peck Rolling Mills in Montreal should be levelled up to the rates prevailing throughout the rest of the industry.
The National Steel Car corporation established a plant in Montreal. They pay forty-five cents an hour in Hamilton and 30-7 cents an hour in Montreal. Quebec is a low-wage province. We hear much about national unity, and yet wages in Quebec are much below those in other parts of Canada. This tends to create in the minds of the people of that province the thought that they are not being treated exactly the same as the rest of Canada.

Industrial Disputes
This is, in my opinion, one of the reasons for any disunity which may exist among certain sections of the French-speaking people. I could discuss this question for perhaps a week if I examined into all the problems. I shall, however, deal only with contentious matters.
A few months ago the hosiery workers in Oshawa went out on strike in an effort to have redressed what I consider were legitimate complaints. The wage rates ran from sixteen to thirty-seven cents an hour. These people did not understand the working of the conciliation machinery-one must have some legal understanding in order to interpret these orders in council-and for that reason they perhaps got away on the wrong foot. They went out on strike, and the minister instructed them as to the necessary road to travel. The result was that they returned to work and applied for a conciliation board in the ordinary way. Since the board was set up, something else has been done to antagonize them. A commissioner was appointed to examine into why the trouble developed. He is investigating the officials who are making an attempt to present the facts in a reasonable way to the board. This only leads to confusion.
This is why strikes occur. As I said before, 75 per cent of these disputes are in the unorganized sections of industry. In the final analysis, what is a strike? It is simply the result of the accumulation of grievances over a period of years. Restrictive legislation and other matters place the employees in a position where they cannot exercise their rights as citizens and express their opinions. I have never found a member of a labour union who was not ready to recognize a problem that really existed. These grievances pile up, and finally someone comes along and gives the needed leadership. I do not think any of these people want to break the law; it merely happens that someone comes along who is prepared to take responsibility and a strike develops.
We have a situation like this at the present time in Toronto. Only this morning the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) asked the minister about a strike in the General Electric plant at Toronto. These people have not union recognition, and they do not know the rules. Many of us who have made a study of these matters are not as clear on them as we should be. As a result, confusion now exists at that plant. I believe the minister stated that a delegation was in Ottawa at the present time to see him in connection with this problem. Some people are going to get into trouble because they accepted leadership in order to bring their grievance to the attention of those in authority. There are perhaps
three or four hundred who have grievances which they want to discuss. In my opinion the way to handle this whole situation is not by 'bringing in a bill like this which merely restricts the right of the working people to have proper representation upon these boards.
The Department of Labour is one of the most important war departments because it has jurisdiction over the hundreds of thousands of workers in this country who are turning out the raw materials necessary for the proper prosecution of the war, and what the Minister of Labour has to do, as an hon. member said this morning, is to accept responsibility for the administration of his department, stand on his own feet, and keep as closely in touch as possible with those who represent organized labour in Canada to-day. I know that they are reasonable and want to travel the right road. Take, for instance, the Congress Journal or the Canadian Unionist, the two official organs of the two major unions in Canada, and you will find that they have mapped out a constructive programme of advice to those who are attempting to handle the affairs of labour through the department. If the road mapped out by them were put in order of council form or in a bill, and brought before this house and the Minister of Labour were given complete jurisdiction over his department and told to go ahead and cooperate with the workers in order to get the best effort possible at this time, this would go a long way towards clearing up our present difficulties.
As I view the situation, however, there are things holding back the Minister of Labour. There are advising him people who have the wrong viewpoint, and a lack of knowledge of the particular problems which the minister must have if he is to find a solution which will put the relations of labour and industry on a sound basis in Canada as they are in England. I think Ernest Bevin in England is the most important man in the British government because he has the confidence of the organized union movement 100 per cent, and the workers in England are prepared to relinquish many of the rights which they have fought over a long period of years to gain, and to place them in the hands of Mr. Bevin on the assurance that, after the war, a new England, and perhaps a new Canada, will be -built and that what they relinquish will then be handed back to them. They are relinquishing those rights because they have confidence in him.
We should do that with the Minister of Labour at Ottawa, but the way to do it is not to tie him up with restrictive legislation such as we have here. I could cite case after
Industrial Disputes

case, and I bring these matters to the minister's attention only in order that we *may get down to basic principles and endeavour to set up an organization through which the working people will be given an opportunity to express themselves. I believe that 90 per cent of the trouble in all our industries across Canada to-day is on account of the fact that the working people are denied the right of sitting in with the management. I know from my own experience of thirty years in unions that the employees will always be reasonable if the case of the employer is properly understood. The Dominion Iron and Steel Company in the Sydney Mines section

 and if the hon. member for the district were here he would corroborate what I say-when it went into liquidation in 1932 called in the union membership and said: "You have to take a 25 per cent reduction in wages if this industry is to continue".

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Has the hon. member in mind that a great number of plants have shop committees of the employees, and is it not a fact that the companies receive advice from these shop committees and consult with them, as I think they should?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: I am speaking, not about company unions but about legitimate union movements.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: I am speaking about workers' associations in the shops.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
That is right. As I was proceeding to point out to the minister, when lit was shown that a section of that industry was insolvent, the workers took a 25 per cent -reduction in their wages. I think they were more reasonable than they should have been because the bondholders' holdings were made good, and the workers worked at reduced wages for two years, to put the industry back on its feet, and are still slowly climbing back to the wages they received in 1932.
The same thing was true in Pictou county, where the workers had $125,000 taken directly out of their pay envelopes -to put -that industry back on its feet. That could never have occurred were it not for the fact that there was a recognized union whose representatives could sit round the conference table with the employer and take back a message to the employees.
What is happening in the General Electric company's plant at Toronto to-day? The workers have nowhere to go, no organization through which to present their oase, and as a result they are out on the street trying to find a solution. Their wages and working conditions are not what they should be, but they have no way of bringing the matter to the attention of those in authority.
[Mr. Gillis.J
In the final analysis, those in industry are largely responsible on account of the antiunion attitude they take. They fail to recognize the fact that the very democracy which they exercise so freely themselves they deny to their employees. The mining industry of Ontario is solidly organized and represented by a general mining association. Dominion Iron, Steel and Coal is organized for the three maritime provinces one hundred per cent through their associations. The general merchant is represented through merchants' associations. The boards of trade represent commercial enterprises. There is a bankers' association. Every phase of our economic life is organized with the exception of the industrial and agricultural workers, and every stop-block that can be put in the way to deprive them of that right is used.
I should like to warn the operator. While he may be afraid that if the workers are organized and start to bargain collectively, they may cut into his profits 5 or 10 per cent, yet if the operators continue to travel the road they are travelling at the present time and to terminate democracy, then before this war is over they may lose much more than they would lose by recognizing the rights of the organized workers. That is something which they must face at the present time, and my advice to the minister, if he wants to do something, is very simple.
First, I think the conciliation machinery should be speeded up. A board is applied for, and months go by before it makes its report. That makes the workers a prey for any subversive elements that wish to exploit their unrest. I have no hesitation in saying that 90 per cent of the workers who go on strike do not do so because they want to strike and be idle. They have many troubles; when they do go out on strike, the subversive elements are apt to play on the men and exploit their unrest and the next thing one finds is that a bad situation has arisen. All that could be cured by setting up legitimate unions. Therefore I say that, first of all, the conciliation machinery must be speeded up. There is no reason why a board should take months to get down to the facts of the case and make its report.
Second, there is order in council P.C. 2685. Those regulations have been passed, and it is simply a matter of putting teeth into them. The Minister of Labour would be one of the biggest men in Canada if he rose in his place, accepted responsibility one hundred per cent and, in cooperation with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), said that that order in council is going to have legal status from now on, and a proclamation was issued that industiy shall recognize the right of the

Industrial Disputes
workers to organize and from this date on accept committees of its employees through their legitimate representatives.
I think order in council P.C. 7440 must be clarified. It should really be repealed, but, if not repealed, it should at least be amended and a new start be made. It has many drawbacks.
I should like in closing to leave this thought with the minister and to make this plea. All our outstanding disputes could easily be cleared up. The situation at the Peck Rolling mills could be cured very easily. The workers in Quebec should be assured that their right to the same wage levels as prevail throughout the rest of Canada is recognized. Stop the situation in Toronto at the General Electric plant before it spreads to many other industries in wat city where the workers, are endeavouring to do the same thing. In the Chrysler plant at Windsor many men lost their jobs, and some of them have not yet been reinstated. These little odds and ends should be cleared up and a new start made. I know that the workers will go down the line with any man who they think is honestly interested in their welfare. The workers axe reasonable, and they, will assist the Minister of Labour in doing what should be done, provided he accepts responsibility.
I regret having to take up the time of the house; but in view of the fact that I am closely associated with the unions, know their point of view, and understand what they want, I wished to make a general statement in order to sum up the situation so that the Minister of Labour or any members of the government who might be labouring under the delusion that certain palliatives of the kind proposed in the bill will remedy matters might have their minds disabused of that idea. Every time you patch the thing you make it worse. A new start must be made on the basis I have indicated. We must do a good job once for all, so that we shall forget all the sectional difficulties and quarrels that beset us and put our minds to the main issue of producing machines and placing them in the field in order that we may defeat those whose intention it is to regiment us and deprive us of those rights that we have now, including the right of every one of us to rise in his place in this house and discuss matters with the rest of the members.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
I have giyen some study to this matter, and I should be glad if the hon. member would elaborate a little. What is the clarification which he thinks desirable and necessary in connection with order in council P.C. 7440? He ought
to be specific about that, because it has troubled me a good deal to know what the point at issue is. I know the trouble in the rolling mill case. The minimum wage is too low.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
Order in council P.C. 7440 fixed the wage rates' at the 1926-29 level, and every conciliation board that has sat so far has applied that literally. The order in council states that in areas where wages were depressed at that time, the rates could be levelled up, but there never has been any levelling up. A rate of 30-7 cents an hour in the steel industry is a depressed wage, and a strike has been in progress now for a month, an endeavour being made to iron out that situation. In my opinion the board should be instructed definitely that the wages prevailing in the steel industry, in Dominion Iron and Steel, should apply in every province. That would be a clarification. Moreover, the basis for the awards of the board in fixing rates is the cost of living as set out in government statistics. But the order in council also states that any sections which may be exceptional should be taken into consideration and that increases in the cost of living might be applied.
There is unrest at the present time in Nova Scotia, and I have particular reference to the eastern end of the province. The reason I know; and a conciliation board has been sitting there. They took as a basis in fixing the wage rate the fact that the cost of living had risen 7-2 per cent since the outbreak of the war. I know that the union in cooperation with the merchants' association made a cost of living examination embracing practically the whole island of Cape Breton, particularly the area in which about 7,000 organized workers are centred, and in that examination they proved to their own satisfaction that there had been an increase of 26-1 per cent in the cost of living in that district. That figure was not their own, because the merchants' association participated in that examination.
If you expect to compensate these people for the increased cost of living by giving them thirty cents a week as a war bonus to offset an increase of 26 per cent in the cost of living, you are bound to have antagonism, and there will be a tendency to fight back. In addition to that, there is the national defence tax, and there are all the other ingredients that go to produce unrest, turmoil and misunderstanding. When a board sits, if the increase in the cost of living is to be made the basis of settlement, that board should make an examination and adjust wages to the increased cost of living. That would be a clarification.
Industrial Disputes

The boards proceed on the assumption that if you were paid twenty cents an hour in 1926-29, that is the prevailing rate in that section, and they go no further. If an understanding were arrived at on these matters, it would in some degree help order in council PC. 7440.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: That was the case in connection with the Peck Rolling mills.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
That is pretty general
throughout.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: So far as I know, no board is prohibited from going into local cost of living conditions if it so desires. That is a matter which is in the discretion of the board.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
Yes; but that has not been done. It will be observed that on the board held in Halifax, one of the first things that the representatives of the men were told, when they sat in, was that order in council P.C. 7440 fixed wages on the cost of living basis of 7-2 per cent, and the board took that for granted. No sectional examination has ever been made.
Again, there is the question of the right of workers to organize. I did think that order in council P.C. 7440 had some merit in those sections where the workers were not organized, in that it instructed conciliation boards to recommend union recognition. I think they gave some legal status to the order in council. That has never been done. There is no recognition in the Peck Rolling mills; the operator is not dealing with them. In the Hamilton situation, where the head of the Hamilton steel company was displaced, there was turmoil. There is no union recognition. The controller placed there by the government still refuses to do business with the union. The government is managing that plant through a controller, but who is controlling the controller? He still refuses to carry out the provisions of the order in council P.C. 7440. There is room for clarification there. Someone must accept the responsibility of coming to an understanding of what these things mean, and so declare.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: There is nothing in order in council P.C. 7440 or P.C. 2685 compelling recognition of the right of collective bargaining. It is purefy a matter of giving freedom, as they have done in England.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
It is a
recommendation.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
Yes; it is a recommendation, and, in the opinion of the government,

if that is done, labour relations will be improved. I believe they will.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST

speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Yes. But note the implication of that, the clear implication is that it is sabotage now, because the situation has not been clearly put and clearly analysed. I say again that that is a libel on labour leadership in this country.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: If that is what it means, certainly it is.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
That-definitely-is what it means. It cannot mean anything else. I am coming to the basis for the amendment with which we are now dealing. The minister used this afternoon the word "technique". It occurred to me that I had seen that word somewhere before, quite recently. In his speech Mr. Justice McTague said:
You often hear of what is commonly called a technique. You all know what I mean. In the last few weeks I think I have been able to detect a new technique in labour conciliation machinery. A certain union applies to the Minister of Labour for a board of conciliation. It represents that it is the accredited bargaining agency for the employees in a certain plant. The fact may be that it does not represent the majority at all.
This is the beginning of the technique. The next step-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, might I interrupt? I did not use the word "technique" in relation to that at all. My reference was to technique in the matter of members of boards, and in the sense that I used it, it had nothing to do with the application for a board.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE THAT MEMBERS OF CONCILIATION BOARDS SHALL NOT HAVE PECUNIARY OR OTHER INTEREST
speechtext:
Just wait a minute. We shall reach, in due time, the matter of the technique with regard to the board. I was dealing only with the first step.
The next step is that the parties appear before the conciliation board and then the question arises as to whether the union represents the men or not.
Industrial Disputes

The union would not raise that question. That question will always be raised by the employer. But here it says that it is the union that raises it.

But why accuse union leaders of using this as a part of their technique?
The union executive then suggests that a vote be taken.
Note this.
The conciliator appointed by the union mildly and subtly suggests that the only fair way to ascertain the disputed fact is for the conciliation board to order a vote.
And then we have this gem:
The chairman and the other conciliator who usually have not the necessary experience to recognize the technique agree and a vote is authorized and held at the expense of the Department of Labour.
Here we get the full basis for the amendment to the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act which we have now before us. The other poor representatives-a judge of a superior court and a well-paid, highly-trained corporation lawyer-these poor innocents do not know what to do when this union conciliator subtly and mildly suggests what should be done; and lo, the vote is taken, and the result is, although the judge does not say so, the employees agree that they want to be represented by the union.
I did1 not wish to bring this out, but there is the reason for the amendment which is now before us.
Then he has something to say about order in council 7440:
To-day government policy as to labour is illustrated by order in council 7440. As a part of the national economy against rising inflationary costs of living, wages are stabilized at the 1926-1929 level or higher thereafter to the date of the order in council. Labour is to be entitled to a flat bonus against rising costs of living- again consistent with the ability of the industry to pay.
I do not think that is in order in council 7440.
In principle, there can be nothing unfair about that in time of war provided the levels in any particular industry were not unfair-and that can be only the rare case. Yet, sometimes, one gets the impression from their conduct that leaders of certain unions are encouraging a deliberate attack on the order in council.
The other day I got a return from the Department of Labour, in which there was a letter written by Mr. Justice McTague to the Minister of Labour. I wish to read that letter. I do not know that the material

tabled is all the information I asked for, but undoubtedly it is all the information the minister could give me. The letter is as follows:
Toronto, April 7, 1941. My dear Mr. Minister:
Dr. Stewart has forwarded to me various documents in connection with the Peck Bolling Mills dispute in Montreal for my formal opinion to you.
The report of the majority of the board is, I think, sufficiently within the terms of P.C. 7440 as now framed that it should not be referred back.
Then there is this paragraph:
However the report confirms me in a view which I have held for some time that it might be advisable to amend the order in council so as to bring it better in line with what I conceive to be general departmental policy.
The last few sentences of the letter are:
As this is a subject having to do with policy I feel that I should do no more than write you personally and confidentially as to the views which I have. Accordingly I am writing you a personal letter on the subject.
Therefore I imagine, there is another letter,
personal and confidential. This one is not so marked; if it were, the minister would be within his right in refusing to table it.
It is regrettable that such things should happen in our country to-day. At the conclusion of his speech Mr. Justice McTague said:
Presently a lot of people are treading dangerous ground. They should be leading in the direction of preparing the way for the aftermath, not sabotaging the present. Canadian labour leaders must handle the situation so that they can look a Bevin or a Morrison or a Greenwood or a Citrine in.the face, and Canadian labour must behave so that it can meet khaki, navy blue or air force blue without the blush of shame. Techniques must be abolished and honest and constructive estimation of facts must take their place.
When I was a young fellow there was a saying that distant fields looked green. I iwould point out that even to-day there are in Great Britain people who are suspicious of Bevin, Morrison, Citrine, Attlee and Greenwood, and who really fear what may happen if Bevin, Morrison, Citrine, Attlee and Greenwood come to power. They fear that more than if Hitler crosses the channel. I wish to say to this house that there are people in this country who are of the same opinion. There are some who are so afraid of social change that they are willing to take a. chance with nazism. They must take their choice, but they cannot avoid 'both.
Having mentioned Mr. Bevin's name, I should like to quote something he said quite recently:
You can easily recreate wealth. You can't recreate liberty once it is gone, nor can you

Industrial Disputes
recreate confidence, the spirit of cooperation and contentment in the heart of the worker after class-hatred once is implanted.
I should like to assist the minister and the government in dealing with the labour questions confronting us to-day, because I believe I know as well as any man in Canada the forces working to subvert labour.
On March 10, I discussed in the house the Hamilton Steel Car situation. I drew attention to the fact that an application for a board had been made on February 3. That situation has not yet been settled. What a field for those who wish to carry on subversive activities! How well is the field prepared for implanting doubt as to the sincerity of the intentions of the government, and the people in industry! Yet, we must deal with those things adequately and quickly, or we shall have more trouble.
There was on'e other difficulty in connection with the Hamilton Steel Car affair. The board took a vote of all employees in the plant with the consent of the company; yet the company refuses to allow the board to deal with any matters except in those particular departments in which the conciliation board was applied for. But there is a conciliation board sitting in connection with a strike at Kitchener. I have in my hand a copy of a letter from the Minister of Labour to the chairman of that board. It is dated at Ottawa, May 29, 1941, and states:
Dear Judge McGibbon:
Re Kitchener strikes
During the course of the day I have been interviewed by several of the Kitchener manufacturers in regard to the labour conditions existing in Kitchener and I am addressing my remarks to you as chairman of the board of conciliation and investigation.
As Minister of Labour I would like to know the reasons behind the trouble in Kitchener and I hereby authorize you to widen the scope of your board into one of investigation and a fact-finding board, so that myself and my department will be fully informed as to the reasons for the existing situation in Kitchener.
I would be glad, therefore, if you would extend the scope of your board to one of a board of inquiry or fact-finding, and report to me the reasons of all the strikes in this industrial centre.
In my opinion, that is a misuse of a board of conciliation. I have no doubt in the world that a fact-finding board in that area, and all over Canada, is needed at the present time. But I doubt very much if Judge McGibbon is the man to undertake it. It should not be undertaken without consultation with labour and employers. Such a commission would be along the lines of the one known as the Mathers commission, which w'ent across Canada in 1919.
The point which I wish to draw to the attention of the house in reading this letter, is that in one plant in Hamilton, where the government has appointed a controller, the employees have asked that the conciliation board investigate the whole of the plant. That request was refused. On the other hand, we. have the request of a few manufacturers from Kitchener, and a conciliation board is set up-

The debate has covered a wide range of matters, and I do not think I should attempt to deal with each individual case which has been investigated by an industrial disputes investigation board. There are quite a number of them, and possibly I could take up one or two now and leave the rest until we are considering the estimates of the department.
I consider that the decision in the Peck Rolling mills case was an unfortunate one, it being based more upon the company's capacity to pay than upon any other basis. The result was that we amended the minimum wage section and raised the rates of pay for those employed in war work throughout Canada. I would point out that the matter of minimum wages is primarily and essentially a provincial one. In other words, the province is responsible for wages.
Reference was made to Kitchener. I may say that the chairman of the board came to see me, and I discussed the matter with him. He told me that he thought the reference was a little limited. He was not referring to it on behalf of industry or on behalf of labour; it was simply as chairman of the board. He asked me if I could widen the scope of the investigation. It so happened that I saw the manufacturers that day, but no suggestion came from them. I deemed it a reasonable request that the board should be permitted to go into not only the petty issue, but any other issues which might be cause for trouble.
The suggestion has been made that the government should make the provisions of order in council P.C. 2865 coercive, that we should compel collective bargaining. The pro-
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
visions of that order in council are not mandatory; they are simply a recognition that in the opinion of the government this would be the best way to produce satisfactory labour relations in war time. If you enter into the field of compulsion on the one side, you have to enter it on the other, and then you stir up inevitable difficulty. One trouble leads to another. If you have compulsory recognition, then you must have compulsory arbitration, and I believe that the labour organizations of this country are not in favour of that.
There are a number of other matters. Reference was made to the address of Mr. Justice McTague, and I am sorry it was thought necessary to bring that up. Mr. Justice McTague enjoys a high reputation as a judge in the province of Ontario and I believe he has proven consistently that he is a friend of labour. I think the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) will agree with that. It is a little unfair to extract one sentence from his speech-

The sentence to which the hon. member paid the most attention was a very brief one. I rather doubt that Mr. Justice McTague meant exactly what the words convey in connection with the lot of workers in Canada. The fact is that his actions do not correspond with those words. I do not believe there has been an occasion where Mr. Justice McTague has not secured the support of the workers in connection with the work of any conciliation board of which he has been a member, and he has been a member of quite a number. He has a wonderful record, and I think in fairness to him I should state definitely that some misconstruction has been placed upon the words he used, perhaps unintentionally. A number of labour leaders have come to me and have told me what a splendid chairman Mr. Justice McTague has made.
I think an almost unfair attempt is being made to give the impression that this bill is directed against labour. It is not. I can state quite frankly that one of the reasons which prompted its introduction was what happened in the Peck Rolling mills case. This bill is not directed against labour in any way, shape or form. The fees paid under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, while perhaps not large, have made it easy for labour to get representation upon these boards. They are not doing it merely for the sake of the money but in order to try to produce peace and harmony. The only purpose of the bill is to see if we cannot rehabilitate the impartiality of the boards and get unanimous

The house in committee on Bill No. 62, respecting Consolidated Fire and Casualty Insurance Company-Mr. Mcllraith-Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.
On section 1-Classes of insurance authorized.

maintopic: CONSOLIDATED FIRE AND CASUALTY INSURANCE COMPANY
speechtext: Would the sponsor of the bill give a short statement explaining its purport?

maintopic: CONSOLIDATED FIRE AND CASUALTY INSURANCE COMPANY
speechtext:
This company was
incorporated in 1930 to carry on a general insurance business. It was authorized by section 6 of the act of incorporation to carry on several different classes of insurance, but the main business was fire insurance. Since that year, insurance practice has changed considerably, and it is now customary to include in a fire insurance policy classes of insurance that were not included at that time. In addition to that, this year the regulations defining the classes of insurance have been amended. These regulations may be found in the Canada Gazette, volume LXXIV, page 3072. The changes in the definition of the various classes of insurance have also made it necessary that the new classes be authorized. Therefore, while certain new classes of insurance appear to be authorized by section 1 of the bill, it is not quite fair to say that those classes are entirely new; part of them are merely covered by the change in definition and by the change in insurance practice. It is impossible to be precise about the extent to which the classes of insurance authorized by the amending section 1 are new.
Section 2 of the bill merely deals with the amount of capital required before the company may engage in any particular class of business. That is made necessary by reason of the changes in the previous section. There is no substantial change; it is a change in form rather than in substance, in order to bring the section dealing with authorized capital into line with the object section of the act.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

The house in committee on Bill No. 66, for the relief of Vivienne Rhodes Whitaker Storey-Mr. Emmerson-Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Right to marry again.

I should like to ask if the
sponsor of the bill, or anyone else who knows, can explain to me the inconsistency between sections one and two, and which is found in all these divorce bills. The first section reads:
The said marriage between . . .
I will not give the names; there is no use in embalming the names of these unhappy people in Hansard. The said marriage between this woman and her husband-
... is hereby dissolved, and shall be henceforth null and void to all intents and purposes
whatsoever.
That seems final and definite. The second section reads:
The said . . .
Giving the lady's name.
. . . may at any time hereafter marry any man whom she might lawfully marry if the said marriage with the said (man) had not been solemnized.
Either that is unnecessary, or else it should have gone further and conferred the same right on the man. If section one is correct when it says that the marriage is null and void, there is nothing more to it; nothing more is needed; but if it is not enough, and it is necessary'' to confer the right of remarriage on the woman, the petitioner in this case, it is also necessary and advisable to confer it

Divorce Bills
on the other party. I would suggest that the form be changed. I do not wish to hold up the bill and have it stopped, but certainly there is an inconsistency.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Unfortunately the other party is able to marry again, too. I have already advocated that there should be a clause that the party against whom the divorce is granted should not be entitled to marry again, but it was not accepted by parliament. Both parties have the same freedom.

At any rate, the bill should
read one way or the other. Now, it seems to throw a doubt: it says that one party may remarry, but it does not say the other may.
The divorce law provides it.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

The house in committee on Bill No. 89, an act for the relief of Ann Elsie Buckley-Mr. Bercovitch

Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.
On section 1-Marriage dissolved.

I want 'to say a few words on this. I am using it only as an illustration to show what a burlesque this procedure is. I have no objection to this particular bill, and I shall not long detain the committee.
The other night the leader of the opposition-

I have to call the attention of the hon. member to the fact that the present procedure is the procedure which must be followed in connection with the adoption of these bills. There is an inquiry into these bills in the senate, and they go before the private bills committee before they come here. I do not think the word "burlesque" should be applied.

I beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman. I will withdraw the word "burlesque". If I can think of a suitable substitute, I shall supply it later on. For the time being we shall call it "the proceedings". I do not believe that the word "burlesque" would be any worse characterization than' this language:
The action of this house in respect of the measure was much more governed by reason and common sense than was the action of the other house.
That was an expression used in the senate about a bill we passed two or three days ago. However, we shall let that go.
The other day the leader of the opposition made the comment that it would be a good thing for the public life of Canada if we had an official equivalent to what is known in the old country as the king's proctor. To those who may not be familiar with that term, I would explain that he was an eminent lawyer appointed to keep a watchful eye on lawsuits, in the public interest, and if he saw a palpable miscarriage of justice he was supposed to intervene. Very often he did so in connection with divorce bills, where he had reason to suspect collusion.
Three things are required in connection with the passage of a divorce bill. These three things must be proved. The first is the matter of domicile. The second is the question of non-collusion between the parties. That is, it must not be a frame-up. The thirdi is that adultery has been committed. Whatever our feelings about divorce may be, that is the law. The law requires these things. It must be proved that there was no collusion. This is generally done by getting the petitioner to make an affidavit. In this particular case this is the affidavit, the statement made under oath:
Q. Is there any collusion between you and your husband with respect to this divorce?
A. No.
Q. Is there any connivance

connivance means consent or acquiescence-in respect of this divorce?
A. No.
That, of course, was made under oalth. Let us look at these facts. I shall recite them briefly, and if hon. members think there has not been collusion-well, then, of course, I am wrong. We find in the evidence that the lady visited her husband some weeks before these proceedings started, and slept in the same bedroom with him. Of course there was no suggestion of arranging a divorce, at all! However, they had a discussion, and she said she was not going to have anything more to do with him. Still, they were quite friendly, apparently-at any rate they slept in the same bedroom.
All this happened at Kingston. I have always understood that Kingston is a place where there are things like hotels, and where they have plenty of accommodation. It was not a case of going out into the bush, and having to occupy the- same place. At that time she was drawing an allowance from her [DOT]husband from the Department of National Defence, because of his being a soldier. She was still drawing it at the time of these proceedings.
The next thing to which I would call the attention of hon. members is the evidence of the detectives. They must have been rank
Divorce Bills

amateurs, from the way they went about their business. Perhaps it is because of my mean disposition that I come to this conclusion, but if there is not a thread of collusion running through this whole thing, then I am badly mistaken. The detectives, or the snoopers as they are sometimes called, consisted of a father and his son. They were of Jewish persuasion, and evidently did not believe in working on Saturday. It will be noted from the evidence that, curiously enough, these things always happened on Fridays. They spotted this man on August 9, again on August 16, again on August 23 and again on September 6-and again, curiously enough, it was always about the same time, namely, a little before six o'clock, or about that.
Just before sundown.

Yes. In the other chamber
somebody has curiosity enough to ask the question as to where this man had been, owing to the fact of his being a soldier. The answer was that he was at Petawawa on the dates mentioned. It was said that he was not on leave on the days in question, with one exception, but that he might have got leave from his commanding officer after the day's work was done. Petawawa is 120 miles from here, and I should think he would have quite a job to get through his work, and get down to Hull, where these things are supposed to have happened-and always to be there around six o'clock. However, the two witnesses agreed that he was there.
When a man goes out to be unfaithful to his wife, he does not generally advertise it. He does not herald it from the housetops. He generally chooses secrecy. This gentleman on the other hand seemed to be almost ostentatious in his infidelity.
Bragging about it.

Finally, in the evidence which is really to the point-and again this is on Friday, the 6th, at 6 p.m.-the detective saw this man, as he put it, go into the hotel and sign the sheet. He does not say what kind of sheet it was. Then they watched. There was the usual performance-I might be reciting the facts of any one of fifty divorces; they all read the same. A man stands to the left of the man who signs the register, and then he is able a few weeks later to swear to it. It is almost phenomenal that they should be right beside the man who signs, and just at the right time-or the wrong time.
Well, at eleven o'clock these two gentlemen went to the door and knocked. I have read some of these divorce cases, and in most of them the gentleman concerned usually chose to be snappy, or had some objection.

Sometimes they even went so far as to tell the other person to get out, sometimes to mention where he could go to, or ask what he was doing there. But that was not the situation here, at all! What happened was this: He went there, and he was received almost with open arms. He knocked at the door and said, "What time are you going back to camp?" And then the evidence continues:
So before I had finished speaking the door was opened by-
Lieutenant So-and-so.
-and when he opened the door I told him I had been watching him on behalf of his wife's solicitor. He said, "What for?" I said, "Divorce proceedings." So we got talking. He said, "You are not going to the camp?" I said, "No." Meantime someone was coming along the corridor, so he opened the door wider and we went inside.
Just a nice, friendly get-together meeting!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A party.

There was no objection, at all. "Come inside", he said, "there is somebody coming down the passageway." Then he was asked to tell the lady's name who was lying there. The answer was that she was Miss somebody-I will not drag her name into it, because I think she is the most respectable of the whole lot.
The proceedings more or less terminated at that point. Does all this not suggest collusion? Read the whole thing through. Apart from all that, I would call attention to the sloppy way-I believe the Chairman will permit me to use that word; we will call it "sloppy"-in which this evidence was collected.
Thus, when these snoopers were watching they saw' the corespondent and the respondent meet together, and "they both shook hands." What kind of lay-out would it have been if only one of them had shaken hands? But all this is solemnly recorded as part of the evidence, as to why this woman should get a divorce. The evidence states that:
.	.	. they both shook hands and went into
the dining room.
They stayed there no less than two hours. Then, we find this later on, regarding the lady, one of them having discovered her as follows-and I would not shock your feelings, even if the house were full of ladies, because she is described in this way:
Her face was bare, and her shoulders -were bare.
Well, you can go to the governor general's assembly in this building and find ladies much more bare than only their shoulders and faces. But, in this case, "Her face was bare"-

United Grain Growers
perish the thought! Yes, "Her face was bare" -what kind of stuff is that? Does that comply with reason and with common sense?
I do not suggest that we should reject this bill, because it was not properly established. We are following the usual sloppy, inefficient, unfair, non-legal way of doing it. But it does suggest a definite need either for a king's proctor or, still better, for amending the laws so that these cases will be tried before courts, where matters of this kind should be taken care of.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend would make a good king's proctor.

I do not wish to give the Minister of Justice an extra job, but I suggest that if he could find some way of taking out of these proceedings provision for the right to marry again, he would find there would not be so many seeking divorces. I know one case of a lady who had been married twice and who wanted a divorce in order to get married again. Such procedure does not make for the upbuilding of Christian homes inj the Dominion of Canada. I do not read through the evidence of these divorce bills, or very many of them; one is enough. We should throw out the whole procedure and bring in something more in keeping with the upbuilding of Christian homes in the Dominion of Canada, and then there would be fewer divorces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend. If we were to eliminate the section giving the right to marry again, the number of divorces would be greatly decreased.

A number of the provinces grant divorces in the courts, not to make it easier but to make it cheaper. I call the attention of members of the House of Commons to the fact that it costs about $50 a minute to have the house sit here. I think it is too much to ask us as members of the House of Commons to spend time in debating this question of divorce when we have nothing at all to do with the manner in which the bills are brought before us. I protest against the whole procedure.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

The house in committee on Bill No. 65, respecting United Grain Growers Limited- Mr. Thorson-Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Characteristics of new shares.
Might we have an explanation of this section from the sponsor of the bill?

This proposed division of the shares and the attaching of certain rights to the divided shares came before the annual meeting of the company in 1039, and the directors were authorized to work out an amendment and devise a plan. The proposed amendment came before a meeting of the delegates in November, 1940, and the request that parliament should be asked to sanction this division of the shares was approved unanimously by the delegates, 284 in number. Some of the details of the plan were objected to by two delegates, but otherwise the approval was unanimous. This division of the shares and the attaching of certain rights to the shares are made desirable on account of certain limitations imposed upon the shares at the present time. Shares can be owned only by farmers or their wives, and this means that when an owner dies or ceases to be a farmer, his shares cannot be transferred to anyone who is not a farmer. The whole scheme has been thoroughly discussed by the shareholders.

I do not wish to oppose the wishes of the majority of the shareholders as expressed at the annual meeting, but there are some observations which I think should be made at this time. This bill destroys the very principle upon which this company was founded in 1911. At that time the farmers wanted to protest against the accumulation of profits of the grain exchange going into the hands of persons other than farmers, and this company was formed for the purpose of having the profits which arose out of the operations of the farmers accrue back to the grain growers themselves. It was originally provided that all shares should be held by farmers and so forth. I have a copy of the minutes of the annual meeting, and an outline is given of the plan of capital stock organization. This is:
For each share of capital stock (par value $25) there be issued one class "A" or investment share, par value $20, and one class "B" voting share, par value $5, subject to the following rights and limitations.
In carrying out the division not more than four class "B" or voting shares will be allotted to any one shareholder. To the extent his present holdings of shares will permit and subject to the consent of the directors, a shareholder may elect to receive "A" (investment) shares only.	.
These are the qualifications with respect to class "A" or investment shares:
Dividend-the right to a preferred dividend as earned (non-cumulative) of five per cent.
United Grain Growers

The bill does not contain that qualification; the rate of 5 per cent is not mentioned in the bill. There is no restriction on ownership, but the restriction on holdings is limited to 250 shares. They would have no voting rights and would be redeemable by purchase at market price, or, on call, at $24 a share. A preferred dividend of 5 per cent is paid upon the investment shares, apparently in lieu of their having the right to vote. Subsection 2 of section 2 is out of line with what the annual convention of last November demanded. I maintain that this bill does not express the wishes of these people. For the past week I have been trying to get in touch with some of the shareholders of United Grain Growers Limited, but, as was the situation with ten other companies to which I wrote, I could not get a list of the shareholders because they said it was not published. In view of the fact that this subsection is not in line with the resolution passed by the convention, I think we ought to postpone passing this bill until it has been completely ratified in its present form at an annual convention.

The essential character of the company is preserved in every respect. With regard to the other points raised by the hon. member for Yorkton; first, with regard to the preferred dividend, it is true that the rate of the dividend is not specifically included in the bill; but if the hon. member will look at section 1, subsection 2, he will see that the powers which are to be exercised as a result of the passing of this bill must be exercised:
... by the enactment by the directors of the company of a by-law in accordance with the terms _ of -a resolution approved by at least two-thirds of the delegates present .at a general or special meeting duly called for the purpose of considering such resolution and held either before or after the passing of this act.
That resolution was passed at the annual meeting in November, and therefore the resolution and the plan that was adopted at that annual meeting become the foundation for the whole bill. Therefore in that way the rate is fixed by implication.
Might I ask whether the resolution was passed by a vote of the delegates at the convention?
Yes.

We were informed in the private bills committee as to the number of delegates present. Perhaps it might assist this committee to know the number of delegates who were at that meeting and whether they were unanimously in support of the resolution.
[Mr. Castleden.l
There were 284 delegates present at the annual meeting, and I think every local in the company, with the exception of three, was represented at the annual meeting.
By voting delegates?-

By voting delegates. The resolution to divide the shares was passed unanimously without a dissenting voice. The resolution approving the plan was passed by all the delegates with only two dissenting votes.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Shareholdings of delegates, etc.
I think this bill should have been sent to the banking and commerce committee instead of to the private bills committee. I do not know why it was ever sent to the private bills committee.

May I ask the sponsor if this bill will get over the difficulty that was faced on account of the fact that the shares are to be owned by farmers or lessees or farmers' wives or farm owners? Will the same difficulty not arise later on when some of the present owners of the shares die, or does the bill take care of that?

I think the passing of this bill will bring the character of the company more in line with its essential purpose of being exclusively a farmer-owned company, because the shares to which voting rights are attached will be reduced in their value and can therefore be more easily sold to farmers than the present existing shares.

That is quite true, that the farmers are going to have control, but the majority of the profits accruing from the operations of the company will go into the hands of those who are going to hold the preference shares, and they do not need to be farmers. One preference share valued at $20 and one common share at $5 are to be substituted for each old share. The information given to the private bills committee was to the effect that almost half the original shares had passed into other hands through farmers dying or retiring or willing these shares to someone else, and that they were not now in the hands of actual farmers. Those who hold or can get control of these shares, which are probably worth nothing if t'he holders are not farmers, will immediately have shares in their hands to the value of perhaps $25 or $30, and the information given to us in the committee was that within the past two years some of these shares have sold for

United Grain Growers
as low as $6 and $6.50. The market for the shares of such a company is restricted to farmers, and the price of the shares is a reflection of what is happening to agriculture, in the west particularly. The farmers have no money to invest in anything. They are trying to keep alive. But if the shares do start paying dividends, say of $1.50 a share, there may be farmers who would be willing to pay $1.50 for them; and if the company is left as it is, the agricultural population will benefit from its operation as one of their own businesses. Is it not true that the largest share of the profits of the company will be in the form of preferred dividends to the people who own the preference or class A shares?

The hon. member forgets that all the holders of these shares will receive, in return for the shares they now hold, two shares, one of which will be the voting share, and the other the investment share.
I stated that.
That should answer my hon. friend's question.

I do not quite follow the argument of the hon. member for Yorkton when he says that this is going to restrict the number of shares held by farmers. I am not a western farmer, but I have followed this bill carefully through the private bills committee, and as I see it, this bill is going to result in a much wider distribution of these $5 shares. Farmers are not precluded from investing in the dividend shares, the preference shares, if they wish to invest in them. I think the hon. member ought to think the matter over a little more carefully.
How many shareholders are there at the present time, how many were there when the company was first incorporated, and what is the present value of the shares?
The number of shareholders as at August 1, 1940, was 26,850, and the book value of the shares was approximately $40.
Would the hon. membei tell us what dividends which have been paid in the last four or five years, going back, say. to 1936?
With regard to the last four years, no dividends were paid in 1937, 1938 and 1939, but in 1940 five per cent was paid.
The hon. member said that the book value of the shares was $40. What is the market value?
The market value prior to 1929 ranged from $25 to $30, but since then the market value has gone to as low as $6.50 a share, and they are currently selling at around $9.
Has the sponsor of the bill any idea of what the value of these shares will be after this legislation is passed?
No one can foretell the future value of shares.

I may be pardoned for intervening in the discussion since for twenty-two and a half years I was president and general manager of this company. The hon. member for Yorkton is, ,1 am afraid, not very well informed either upon the history of the company or upon the provisions of this measure.
I was merely trying to get some information.

The company was incorporated, not in 1911, but in 1906, by letters patent issued in the province of Manitoba. It then sought dominion incorporation by special act of parliament in 1911, and that act of parliament was, as I recall it, further amended in 1916.
This company started as a farmers' company. There were definite and strict limitations in the matter of qualifications for the holding of stock. Only farmers and farmers' wives were eligible to be shareholders, and the par value of the shares was $25. In the early years from 1907 to 1917 or 1918 the company secured by far the greater number of its shareholders. The hon. member for Selkirk has given the number at the present time. Consequently we had in the early years of the company thousands of shareholders scattered over the prairies, all farmers, since only farmers could qualify as shareholders. Many, however, did not remain farmers. Some left the farm and went into business, becoming merchants or implement dealers or preachers or school teachers or something else, and so passed from the rigid qualification of farmer into some other class.
As time went on, many of the shareholders died, and there arose the problem of the disposal of shares by their estates. That accounts for the remarkably low value which the shares reached a few years ago. On any reasonable valuation of the assets at the present time, the shares are worth from $35 to $40. Why then does the farmer who wants to sell his shares not receive that amount? He cannot on account of the limited market there is for them. It may be that the depressed conditions of agriculture
363S
United Grain Growers

have militated against the ability of executors of estates to find a market for the shares among those qualified to hold them.
It is that very condition which, this bill proposes to cure, as I understand it. At the same time, it retains the essential principle whereby the farmers continue to hold control of the management and direction of the company. Shares of a new class are created which may be held by merchant or preacher or anjmne else, but the return which they can get on those shares is limited to 5 per cent. That is not an unreasonable return to people who have invested their money, having supplied the capital that went into equipment, buildings and other necessities which the company required.
I may tell the hon. member for Yorkton, if he has studied the history and practice of the large cooperative organizations in Great Britain, where they have carried the cooperative idea to a greater extent than we have ini Canada, he will find that one of the essential provisions in their charter to do business is that the first charge on profits is a return on capital invested; and a few years ago, and I presume it is still the situation, this provided a return of 6 per cent. In this case the company proposes to give to those who supplied capital, under this new arrangement with regard to shares, a return of 5 per cent, and I do not think that can be regarded as unreasonable. Thus the limitation is 5 per cent return to those who may hold shares of the class described in the bill, and the essential principle is retained that the control and direction of the company remain in the hands of farmers and cannot be taken away from them.
The bill is a necessary measure to meet the changed conditions that have arisen through the change in the ownership of the stock and the movement away from the essential provisions in the charter of incorporation. that only farmers should hold stock. It simply provides a means of rearranging that, retaining the vital principle of control.

I thank the minister for his explanation. I did use the word "organized", and I suppose I should have said "constituted", in 1911. I believe the minister left out two other dates. There were amendments in 1915 and 1918.

And in 1918 as well. The point is that the profits accruing out of the operation of United Grain Growers Limited, through this bill, can now go to persons who are not farmers. Like the minister, a good many farmers who were originally

in the business have gone into some other occupation, being no longer engaged in agriculture. I should like to have a statement of what percentage of the shares-are there not
26,000	shareholders?-are in the hands of farmers, and the number that are not.
I do not know that I can give the exact percentages, but the number of shares that are not in the hands of farmers is only a very small fraction of the total.
Approximately what?
I do not think I can give the figures. I believe there are only one or two thousand.

That is, at
present?
Yes.
What will it be after the bill goes through?

The reason why these shares are not in the hands of farmers is that, in most instances, they belong to estates, and the beneficiaries of the deceased holder of the shares cannot be registered as shareholders because they are not farmers. I think I can safely say that the number of shares which are not held by farmers is very small. After this bill passes, for each share that now exists there will be two-one which will be the voting share, which cannot be held by anyone except a farmer, and the other which is the investment share and which may be disposed of. What will happen in the course of time with regard to that, no one can tell.
The hon. member says that a number of these shares are now in the hands of estates. What has happened to the dividends which were payable on those shares?
Any dividends applicable to those shares cannot be paid to anyone, because in respect of those shares where the owners are not farmers they cannot be registered as transferees.

Then I take it that
the profits which have accrued for the past few years have been distributed among the shareholders who are real farmers?

Or are they in a trust
fund?

I am not sure on that
point.

If they
are not paid they would be held as unpaid dividends.

United Grain Growers
On section 7-Acquisition of shares.

I have read this bill with a good deal of care, and I understand there is real necessity for the passing of the bill. The only clause in it that I queried in my mind was this one. This, of course, is a real departure from the principle governing joint stock companies, because it provides that shares in the company "to the ownership of which there is attached the right to take part in the selection of delegates or the right to act as delegate shall not by devolution or otherwise become vested in persons disentitled to exercise the rights aforesaid". Then it goes on to provide that the company may purchase those shares under certain limitations. Provision is made for resale by the directors of any shares acquired under subsections 1 and 2. The fourth subsection provides for a limitation of purchases so that:
No shares shall be acquired under this section so as to increase the number of shares acquired and not resold hereunder beyond one-tenth of all the outstanding shares of the same class.
That, of course, is a distinct departure from the ordinary principle governing joint stock companies whereby a company cannot purchase its own shares.
I mentioned this to the counsel whom I queried about it, and he was very frank and told me that it was not absolutely essential to the immediate objective of the company, and that he was fully appreciative of the danger of the clause in ordinary joint stock company organization. But he pointed this out, and this is a consideration which I should like to pass on to the committee; that the fundamental conception of the company was that it should be controlled by farmers, with voting rights limited to one man one vote, regardless of the share holdings, with the distinct limitation on the number of voting shares which, one person might hold; and that this removed any temptation to manipulate the market either to secure control or for speculative purposes. Of course that is true; it would be an effective deterrent from attempting to get control or to manipulate. He further asserted to me that the company is cooperative in nature, organized to serve the western farmer, and it is a principle of legislation affecting cooperatives that they can cancel the membership of any member if he ceases to be one of that class. They are not, however, asking for any such power as that of cancellation. This is the method they have adopted, under advice of counsel I understand, whereby a market may be provided
for the shares of deceased persons which cannot be transferred to or registered1 in the name of other than a farmer.
The market for these shares must be more or less limited. Therefore they have asked for this right. I am informed that in the committee of the other house where this bill was examined with considerable care, perhaps a good deal more than we can give here in this committee, the suggestion was made that the company should have even wider powers than those provided by the bill, as a means of getting rid of members who are no longer active farmers, so that the company would be definitely owned and controlled by activ.e farmers.
I am not opposing the bill; from the explanation given me I think it is necessary; but I thought it right that the committee should understand just what the underlying principles of section 7 are. It is a very unusual power; I never saw it in a bill before; it is expressly prohibited by the Companies Act. With that explanation, however, I think it . might go through.

Would the sponsor of the
bill inform the committee as to the number of directors and who they are?
I have not that information at the moment. I wonder whether that is relevant to this section. I shall be glad to obtain it for the hon. member.

they do as directors. The officers of the company do.

I shall have to obtain
that information also. I shall be glad to do
so. But it does not really touch the section.

They have two terminal
elevators, one at Port Arthur and one at Vancouver.
