21/6. Audit of revenue, money order, postal note and savings bank business; issue of postage stamps and postal notes, including amounts required to pay allowances to office appliance operators grade 2, in accordance with regulations approved by order in council, $1,408,700.
Will the minister explain the increase?

Yes. According to the estimates, an increase of $126,795 is shown in this item. Actually there were supplementary items last year; and when the supplementaries are added to the estimates of last year, the actual increase for this year is $87,195. The increases are these: First of all, the salary item, $16,230, which includes statutory increases amounting to $13,770; one additional clerk, grade 1, $720, and a postal clerk, $1,740. There are two positions dropped, so that this represents, in the total salary account, a net increase, on that item, of $13,195. The next one is printing and stationery, showing an increase in the estimates, but, if the supplementary estimates of last year are included, a decrease of $2,250. In equipment and maintenance there is an increase of $45,000. The particulars are available; would the leader of the opposition like to have them?
No.

Other increases are: in
sundries, $850; in the manufacture of postage stamps, $23,400; in printing of postal notes, $7,000. In all these figures there is taken into consideration the fact that the supplementary estimates are added to the estimates-which really gives the true position so far as the increases are concerned.

Of course the supplementary estimates show there was an increase last year. I understand that this item was kept open because somebody might wish to ask a question on some other item. The only question I desire to ask with respect to the post office is, how the country is going to determine whether the post office is a losing or a paying proposition, having regard to the large sum of money which is expended

Supply-Post Office
by business and others in the purchase of stamps for excise purposes. This, I know, is an old story and an old question, but we shall never know whether the post office is on a sound and proper basis until we can have some estimate, even though an approximation, of how much money in revenue the post office gets from the purchase of stamps which should go to the excise branch. Many people use postage stamps when properly they should use the excise stamps. Occasionally I do so myself, although in business we always try to purchase the special excise stamps. In my view, as this amount may be very large, there is no knowing how the post office is breaking. I think we should have some check on that, in order to know exactly what the position is.

I know the leader of the opposition realizes the difficulty of obtaining
any accurate statement on that point.
Yes.

If one tried to figure it out and keep track of each one of the transactions, the cost would be out of all reason. There is, however, some information available. First of all, 75 per cent of the business comes from city offices, and the banks and the merchants in general use excise stamps and not postage stamps in those centres.
I think likely that is true.

The remaining 25 per cent comes from offices of lesser revenue where excise stamps are not so much in use. The use of postage stamps is a great convenience to the public in the rural districts, but the number used for excise purposes is not very great.
"Not very great." Is that a statement of fact or an assumption?
That is the opinion of the officials.
That is an assumption.
So far as they can find out from a careful check-up on the situation.
I think it is just an assumption.

To get definite figures it
would be necessary to establish a fairly complicated accounting system, and, when one got through, it would not be of any advantage to the public from a financial point of view.
It would cost a good deal of money without bringing any additional revenue to the country.
Agreed.

The use of postage stamps as affecting revenue is relatively very small, but it is a great service to the public in many places since it facilitates the transaction of business. I understand the desire of the leader of the opposition to obtain an idea of the approximate amount, but I believe he also realizes that the cost would be out of all proportion to the benefit to 'be derived.

I agree with that general statement; and of course, the statements made by the Postmaster General are also general. Is there any approximation of the amount? Would it run to a million a year? Have the officials made some check on the city offices?

The officials say that they would not like to make any statement as to the actual amount. It might be possible for us to put on a check on the city offices, without too much expense-if we were to pick out different days on which to do it. But we could not do it over a period of time, because it would tie things up considerably.
We shall have to give it up.

I believe the minister is most anxious to expedite the delivery of mail, because the more quickly mail is carried, the more mail service will be used. I recently had occasion to go by train from Ottawa to Pembroke and return. In each case I travelled on a train which carried mail. From my experience that day I would say that the people of the Ottawa valley are most shockingly treated by the mail service-and of course that is not the responsibility of the Post Office Department. I refer to the mail service on the train. I am finding fault, not with the postal employees on the train, but rather with the train service itself.
The afternoon train leaves Pembroke at 1.45 p.m. and is supposed to leave Carleton Place at 4.15 p.m., having arrived there a half hour earlier. But for some time past, the train from Pembroke upon reaching Carleton Place must stand there waiting for the train to arrive from Toronto.
Three quarters of an hour.

That train is frequently late. Four coaches, including a mail coach, are taken from the Toronto train. That train left Carleton Place at 5.20 p.m., and, I

Supply-Post Office

suppose, arrived in Ottawa about 6.30 p.m. A wayfreight would carry mail more quickly than this mail train, so-called, carries it. In my judgment the postal authorities should take note of these facts, because I am told by many people that it is a regular occurrence. The department should see that the people of the Ottawa valley receive more expeditious mail service than is now accorded them.
I believe the hon. member for Davenport will realize that this is really a transport matter.
Yes; but the minister's department should make them speed up.

We make representations from time to time to the board of transport commissioners, asking them to speed up service, in so far as our mails are concerned. I thank the hon. member for having brought this matter to our attention, and I can assure him we shall be glad to make further representations.

I was about to ask about the post office savings bank. How many depositors have we, and what would the average deposit amount to? Let us have some idea of what our savings bank business amounts to. I ask the question because I hold the opinion that a great deal could be done, and particularly in the country districts, to encourage the post office savings bank. Many of our towns have no banking facilities whatever, and I should think we might be able to extend the post office savings bank business, and develop it into something which would give service to people in communities where there are no banks.
The aggregate balance to the credit of depositors on March 31, 1941, was $22,176,632.54. The number of offices authorized to transact business was increased from 1,645 to 1,664.
What interest is paid?
What are the qualifications necessary to conduct an office?

If the hon. member wishes, I can place on record a short statement.
Mr.	COLD WELL:	That would be
satisfactory.

The aggregate balance to the credit of depositors on March 31, 1941, was $22,176,632.54, a decrease, during the year, of $923,485.90. The average to the credit of each depositor was $225.96, compared with $246.90 on March 31, 1940.

New accounts opened during the year numbered 11,189, and 6,606 accounts were closed, leaving the number open at the close of the year, 98,144, or an increase of 4,583.
The deposits were 81,532 in number, for a total amount of $3,998,091.16. The average amount of each deposit was $49.04 compared with $53.21 for the previous year.
Repayments numbered 102,447 and amounted to $5,355,477.82, of which 92,669 for a total of $2,383,030.82 were made in cash, and 9,778 amounting to $2,972,447.00 were made by cheque. The average cash repayment was $25.72 compared with $25.64 the year before, and the average withdrawal by cheque was $303.99, compared with $313.40 in the preceding year.
What are the requirements by which a post office becomes a savings bank office?

Generally, where there are no other banking facilities, when application is made it is granted, provided, first of all, that the official at the point in question is able to carry on a savings bank business and capable of performing the duties of looking after it. The second consideration is that satisfactory premises are available at the point indicated.
I was wondering where these funds are invested. Presumably they are invested with the government, or are retained in one of the government funds; is that correct?
They are placed to the credit of the consolidated revenue fund.
Then they are accessible for use by the dominion?
Yes.

It seems to me that we have been looking round for ways of increasing our financial resources during war time; here is one way. When the Minister of Finance brought in his budget, and previously when we were discussing the unemployment insurance measure, one of the reasons given for the desirability of setting up that fund at this time was that it would enable the government to obtain more money during the war. Here we have a channel which, it seems to me, we are not using as we ought to be using it. The government of New Zealand -not the present Labour government, but the previous government-fostered the post office savings bank until it became an institution which was exceedingly worth while from the point of view of the government itself. I have often thought that here was a channel which might be used.

Supply-Post Office
In some cities, hundreds of school children and students are encouraged to open savings accounts in their own names. These accounts are usually handled by one of the chartered banks, and the result is that these children become acquainted with the bank, and many of them continue to do business for the rest of their lives with the same bank. One of the ways of building up the post office savings bank would be to encourage the children now using these penny-banks to put their money in the post office savings bank. Ten or twelve years ago we had a superintendent of schools in Regina, who happened to come from this city and who instituted* a penny-bank system. I do not know how much money they have in that bank at the present time, but when I left the teaching profession in 1034 there was some S50,000 in the savings accounts.
The teachers in these institutions are public servants who are performing a voluntary service, first, for the children and, second, for the private banking institutions. I have heard it stated on more than one occasion by the teachers that they would feel more enthusiastic if they were performing this service for the post office savings bank or some other public institution. I bring up this matter so that it may be considered by the department. We should encourage our children to open accounts in the post office savings bank in order that they may continue to be customers in future years.

The hon. member will notice that there was a drop of approximately $1,000,000 in the savings accounts, but that is due chiefly to the fact that people were withdrawing money to buy war savings certificates, war savings stamps and things of that kind. The rate of interest paid is 2 per cent, and it might be interesting to note that last year the interest amounted to $433,900.76, of which only $11,586.05 was paid out, the balance of $422,314.71 being added to principal by the different depositors.
They were really saving the interest?
Yes.
How many postmasters were guillotined last year?
There were none guillotined, but if the leader of the opposition wishes any particular information, I shall see if I can get it.
I am not going to pursue that.

Following up the question asked by the leader of the opposition, I should like to make a complaint on behalf of the returned soldiers in my constituency. I have received a number of complaints from these men that they have not received consideration when new appointments or changes were made. It is true that announcements go out to the provincial command in Regina; but in a constituency such as the one I represent, where we have poor mail service and poor communication, some of the legion secretaries may be living eight or ten miles from town; they do not receive their mail regularly, and many of them have no telephone connection with the other officers of the legion. Even if a secretary is advised that a change is about to be made in a post office in the district, possibly twenty-five or thirty miles away, it is not always possible for him to notify veterans living in the community that a change is about to be made. Would the minister take greater pains to see that returned soldiers are notified more directly.
Just a year ago I appealed to the veterans in connection with the national registration, and they responded in a remarkable manner. At the present time they are cooperating in connection with the war loan. On every count these returned veterans are coming across, but there is keen resentment when appointments are made without their being notified. I do not expect the Postmaster General to recommend the appointment of returned soldiers when they do not possess the necessary requirements, but in man}'' of these communities there are returned soldiers who have the necessary requirements and yet they do not seem to be given an opportunity of making an application until it is too late. A recent change has been proposed in one post office, and I am told that the suggested postmaster is not a returned soldier.

I shall be glad to look into the hon. member's statement and would be pleased to have him give me particulars of those places in his constituency where there is poor mail service. I should like to have that investigated to see who is to blame. I am advised by my officials that in every case a notice is sent to the provincial command of the Canadian Legion in advance of any appointment being made. In connection with the case referred to by the hon. member, the file shows that no returned soldier applied for the position, and so far as I have been able to ascertain, no representations were made on behalf of any returned soldier.

I am not complaining about the poor mail service. In many parts
Supply-Post Office

of my constituency there is a mixed train only three times a week. As I pointed out, some of these people live eight to ten miles from town and possibly go in only once a week for mail. While I realize that notice would be sent to the provincial command in Regina, the fact is that it might be a month before this information would reach the secretary and then go from him to the returned soldier's in the community. In the particular case I complained about, I do not suggest that word did not go to Regina; all I say is that the returned soldiers in that community are complaining that they had no knowledge that a change was being made. Naturally they resent having an appointment made without being given an opportunity to submit an application.

I think every effort
should be made during war time to get away from this pernicious patronage system. It is galling to a man who is qualified to take charge of a post office to be told by some petty village politician that he will never get it because he did not vote right. I know of a number of cases like that. We are being asked all the time to get our people to assist in salvage campaigns, recruiting campaigns, the sale of war savings certificates and so forth, and yet these things happen. I have had men say to me, "You asked me a year ago to give my services or my house for registration purposes, and I did so, but I see now that in other fields, the census, for example, or when a post office comes up, the same old gang round here profess to have the political patronage." We should get away from that.
Having given the department something like a kick perhaps, may I say that I appreciate the action taken in one instance I know of in my own constituency when tremendous pressure was brought to bear on the minister and the officials of his department to appoint a man who was not qualified. I refer to the town of Biggar. But the minister and his officials did the right thing. They took the recommendation that was made on the qualifications of a returned soldier and appointed him to the position. Having made the other observation, I think it is only fair that I should compliment the minister upon having stood firmly against what I know was tremendous pressure brought to bear by several people in that locality.
I hope the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar does not apply his implications to myself as probably he has done regarding every member on this side.
What is that?
The implication of rottenness.
Oh, no. I was not dealing with members of the house at all. Of course, however, I cannot speak for the consciences of individual members.

The leader of the opposition
asked about the number of dismissals. From July 9, 1940, to March 10, 1941, the total number dismissed was thirty-three, six for political partisanship and twenty-seven for other reasons.
Would the Postmaster General be good enough to give us the gross revenues of the ten largest centres? And would he state beforehand just what the gross revenues include?

It includes postage on all mail matter, the sale of stamps, but not money orders. The revenue in 1939-40 at Calgary was $660,741; Edmonton, $673,242; Montreal, $5,212,180; Quebec, $806,198; Regina, $973,293; Saskatoon, $343,500; Toronto, $7,913,357; Winnipeg, $3,092,225.

The Postmaster General will recall that last summer, along with his able deputy, he visited the city of Windsor and inaugurated an air mail service in that important city. There are now two services a day, one in the afternoon and one in the early evening. I know there are difficulties on account of the Chicago connections, but could not arrangements be made for a morning service, thereby providing added facilities for Windsor and all that area, and increasing the revenue of the department?
Now that the hon. member has drawn the matter to my attention, I will give it consideration.

The Postmaster General undoubtedly has forgotten that I have drawn it to his attention on no fewer than six occasions since last fall. I might refresh his memory by informing him that he told me one of the difficulties was not with his department but with the ministry of transport. Possibly he has had an opportunity of discussing the matter further with the ministry of transport so as to' bring this necessary service to the important city of Windsor.
I can assure the hon. member that I have not forgotten his representations, but all I can say is that I' will give the matter consideration. That is as far as I can go.

Does the ruling still hold good that an applicant for the position of postmaster must have been a patron of that post office?

Generally speaking, yes. That is the general rule, but occasionally there have been exceptions.

Would a veteran living
outside the district be given a preference over a man within the district who was not a veteran?

No. If there was no one
within the district who was capable of performing this sendee, we would have to consider applications from outside, but that is not usual. Offhand I do not know of any case where it was impossible to find someone within the district who was capable of performing the duties.

Is there any way of
knowing whether the postal note division operates at a profit or a loss?
Yes.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
ordinarily in taking up my estimates I would have the first item on the list called and proceed in sequence, but to oblige members of the house and to fulfil an undertaking I gave earlier in the session, I am having this item called in order to give an opportunity to those who desire to speak on wheat and kindred subjects.
That subject has not been discussed at all this session, has it?

As the minister has stated,
he agreed to allow a general discussion on this item, the Canada Grain Act. I discussed this with him on one or two occasions, and he graciously agreed to accord us this opportunity. On one or two occasions since this session opened I have endeavoured to obtain additional information beyond that supplied in answer to casual questions. This house has been in session continually since November 7, except for a short recess at Christmas We have had very little information with regard to the real operations of the wheat board and the grain situation generally. I have here a report dated January 11, 1941, in which there is given a partial record of the workings of the board to that date. Certain amendments to the wheat board act are set out and discussed, and we have had a number of orders in council, which are to all intents
and purposes amendments. But we have not had any amending act, and I object to this way of dealing with the board's operations.
On March 12 we had what might be called a double-barrelled announcement from the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and thereafter we had an order in council tabled by the minister on May 14, and another one recently on May 30 setting out certain regulations to show how the board proposed to operate during the coming crop season. Apart from that, we have had very little information. The report to which I have referred mentions certain amendments of 1939 in which the price was fixed at 70 cents, and it also refers to the amendments of 1940 again setting the price at 70 cents. It then gives a general review of the operations of the board. It is not widely distributed, however, and very few farmers of western Canada have seen it. But even if they have seen it, they cannot get a detailed account of the board's operations.
We have a balance sheet which shows that the 1938 crop was disposed of, and finally there was a loss of $61,000,000. It deals further with the rest of the 1939 crop, showing that there was on hand on July 31, 1940, 182,095,733 bushels of that crop. But there was a deficit up to that time, in the handling of t'he 1939 crop, of $6,000,000 odd. Certain exhibits are set out in the report-A, B and C. Exhibit A, which appears on page 28, sets out the liabilities to the bank, with interest, amounting to $68,825,078. There is a liability to agents of the board for wheat purchased from producers but not yet delivered to the board, the amount being $28,927,925. There is, I presume, interest on that amount. I think we should have some further information with regard to these liabilities, particularly that to the agents of the board.
On page 21 of the report we have a statement to the effect that there are certain liabilities to the agents. It is stated that when wheat is delivered by the producers to the country elevators of the companies who are acting as agents for the board, the companies pay the producers for the wheat on the basis of the board's initial price. The liability continues to be carried by the companies until such time as the wheat is unloaded in deliverable position. These liabilities represent approximately 42,000,000 bushels of wheat carried in country elevator^, in transit at the date of this balance sheet. I think we should have some particulars as to what the amount of this liability is.
This evening I am going to direct certain questions to the minister with a view to

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
obtaining information. He has his two chief officials before him, and he can get the information. I do not intend to hurry. I should like his officers to take notes and give us the necessary information through the minister.
I will not take time to deal with the rest of the report. It is more or less confusing, however, to the ordinary individual. Coming back to some of the orders in council, and what I have called the doublebarrelled announcement of March 12, when the minister made a statement with regard to what might happen in connection with the 1941 crop, I would point out that on several occasions I have tried to get information from the minister, but without avail. He was always taking certain things into consideration, and so far this session he has not given us a proper detailed report indicating the present position of the board and of the entire situation. I might refer to certain representations made to the minister before the announcement of March 12. The federation of agriculture and other interests in the west stated their position when they demanded a better price than 70 cents. They asked what might be called a parity price. We were disappointed that no results ensued from those representations, but that is water under the bridge. In the budget statement, however, reference was made to the present situation, and it was pointed out that the board's present carrying of wheat showed that they would have at the end of the crop year some 570,000,000 bushels of a carry-over. The minister also said that there was $400,000,000 invested in the business and that it was costing the country about $50,000,000 or $60,000,000 a year to carry it.
The regulations which I have here provide for taking out of this year's crop a delivery of 230,000.000 bushels. The regulations are given with regard to deliveries and so forth, but I am not going to take time to-night to discuss them. The regulations have been distributed, and they are pretty well understood by those who will be delivering wheat-the producers-and those who will do the physical handling. Let me refer to the announcement made some time ago with regard to the sale of 120,000,000 bushels of futures to the United Kingdom. At that time it was stated that the sale was made considerably above the then market price, which would be 70 cents, but the minister did not say what the price was. I remember asking him if he would state the price, and he replied that for certain reasons he did not think it advisable nor did the British government wish to have the price announced.

I think the hon. gentleman has made a mistake there, if he will allow me to interrupt. On this occasion, according to my recollection, I did not say anything regarding the amount paid for the grain or the price at which the sale was made. I did not refer to it as being considerably above the market price.
The minister did not give any information at all.

He said it was over the market price. Then I asked the price, and the minister said that it was not in the public interest to announce it, that the British government did not want the price announced.
That is correct.

If it was 70 cents, it would not have been necessary for me to ask. The minister said that there was a request by the British authorities that the grain exchange remain open. I ask him to-night through his official to produce some evidence, real evidence, that that is the situation. I have here the monthly statement by his own department, dated May 23. On page 6 of this we find a statement or chart headed "Liverpool wheat offers", and it shows that for the month of May, the date his statement was made, the price they offered was 91 cents at the port of shipment. Therefore I cannot see why, if they were offering that price-and that is from a document put out by his department-we could not have the exact price. I do not suppose that if they were offering that, the wheat was sold at less.
I quote from a further statement, the weekly bulletin of his bureau, dated May 17:
The export of wheat in April amounted to 20,322,400 bushels at a value of $17,393,126 or an average of 85-6 cents per bushel. This compared with 93-8 cents in April, 1940.
Then during the four months ending April there was an export of 46,284,793 bushels of a value of $39,017,774, or 84*3 cents a bushel. So why not divulge the price?
The hon. member is quoting seaboard prices there.

That is correct, but we know what the freight from Fort William is, and it figures back to much more than 70 cents. It is rather a joke for the minister to say that they cannot divulge this price when Liverpool is advertising it, as is also his own department.
I wish now to refer briefly to another document. Some hon. members may recall that when the budget resolutions were going through and the last item was reached, I asked the Minister of Finance if he would

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
permit me to refer to the appendix in the budget resolutions, and I was refused an opportunity of asking the question. I am now going to refer to that and ask a question. On page 2389 of the ways and means resolutions under the heading "indirect liabilities", paragraph 53 reads as follows:
Guaranteed bank advances to the Canadian wheat board outstanding on March 31, 1941, amounted to $101,052,679. This amount constituted the board's gross liability to the banks and mainly related to the purchase of the 1939 and 1940 wheat crop at the fixed price of 70 cents per bushel No. 1 northern, Fort William. The guarantee of the dominion to the Winnipeg Grain and Produce Clearing Association Limited, referred to in previous budgets, is still outstanding. No liability accrues from day to day in connection with this guarantee as margin deposits are made to the clearing association daily.
I ask the minister to tell us to-night what that guarantee to the Winnipeg Grain and Produce Clearing association is, why there is a guarantee, and if the government is guaranteeing the accounts of those brokers or grain firms that are operating for the board? Also we wish to know what margins the board has to put up in the clearing house. The $120,000,000 referred to a few minutes ago was futures, and we wish to know what margin the board has to put up daily, as referred to here. Also we wish to know what the margins in the clearing house are at the present time. Would it by any chance be that owing to the fact that the wheat board has a guaranteed liability in the Winnipeg clearing association, the government want the grain exchange to remain open? If their account were cleared up with the grain exchange or the clearing association, would they need the exchange to remain open? These are some of the things we desire to know. I wish to know the margins put up, and I think we should have some information with respect to how the board is now operating, whether the funds provided for the board are advances made by the finance department here. Does the board draw on the finance department here daily? I know how Mr. McFarland operated; I know the worry he caused that government on certain occasions. I think we should have the information as to how and why accounts are still outstanding, particularly whether these are guaranteed accounts of the brokers, the rate of interest paid to the grain companies on the grain for which they pay the producer, and also the interest paid to the brokers if they put up money on account of the board.
Coming to this question of closing the exchange, I have made some inquiry and
investigation recently, and I find that statements have been made-this is more or less in reply to the minister when he says that the British government does not want the grain exchange closed. I have here a statement by David Muir, Glasgow manager of the Scottish Cooperative Wholesale, in which he says that there would be no difficulty if the Winnipeg futures market were closed. Another statement is from Mr. A. C. Bracey, buyer for the English Cooperative Wholesale society, Liverpool, in which he says the advantage would be to the western producer if the Winnipeg grain exchange were closed. Another is from the Glasgow Corn association, that if the Winnipeg futures market were closed, there would be one less to watch. Another is from the British National Millers association that they never deal there at all. Yet we have the statement that the exchange is necessary.
I believe the hon. gentleman is quoting letters. I ask that he table all the correspondence from which he is quoting.
I am quoting from sworn evidence given before the royal grain inquiry commission.
That rule has no application; it is only a minister who has to do that.

I am going to make certain references to the board's operations on the Winnipeg grain exchange, and I make this statement, that any institution which is so important in the national life of the Canadian wheat producer and the marketing of Canadian grain, which has been the subject of seventeen inquiries in about thirty years, which is carried on under certain rules and regulations, which is subject to control by no outside body and not even by the government, which does not know the volume of trading each day in it and whether there is speculation and does not know who operates on that exchange, whether operating for the Canadian wheat board or the British government or who, and will not give that information-such an institution of such a character should be closed and taken over by the government for at least the duration of the war.
May I ask the hon. member, simply for my own information, when was the evidence given to which he refers?

It was given before the
Turgeon commission and tabled here in 1938.
I come to these orders in council. The one of May 14 gives directions with respect to the delivery of grain and the time for
May I ask my hon. friend if there is any charge of crooked work now- on behalf of the board?

There are certain things
going on. I will read in a minute or two some of the-few-things that are going on, and you can judge.

speechtext: The hon. member should not use that language.

I will say this. The board is playing into the hands of 'certain interests in Winnipeg. Maybe the company of which the hon. member was vice-chairman-or president and manager for twenty-two years -might be one of them.

If the hon. member will
do me the courtesy of allowing me to make a remark, I should like to say through you, Mr. Chairman, to the hon. member that he has no right whatever to make an imputation of the character he did, that there is crooked work in the administration of the wheat board; and I would ask my hon. friend to withdraw it.

I said that the whole thing
is a racket.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No, no; you used the words that it was crooked work.
I said that it would not bear the light of day, and that we wanted an investigation.
No; you used the words "crooked work".

I said that it would not bear the light of day, and that there were certain things-and I say it again-going on in the Winnipeg grain exchange, with which the 'board has something to do, which will not stand investigation.
I think the hon. member had better be specific.
Oh, well, now, what he has said so far is all right.

What the hon. member said, Mr. Chairman, was that the members of the Liberal party sitting on this side of the house in'1935 demanded that Mr. Bennett bring Mr. McFarland here, and there was no question of crookedness at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Oh, that was not it at all.

The hon. member for
Waterloo South is certainly not helping the situation. He is not helping the hon. member for Qu'Appelle by the explanation he has just given. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle used the words "crooked work"-
Order.
-and carried the imputation that it was being applied to the wheat board.
Definitely not.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Attention was immediately called by the Minister of Mines and Resources to the expression used by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. That expression was immediately challenged, and the hon. member must withdraw it, or prove it before this committee.

speechtext: That the time had come when the crooked work of the officials of the wheat board should be exposed.
No; he did not say that at all.

I was listening very attentively to the hon. member. He said that in 1935 the opposition party had forced Mr. Bennett to bring Mr. J. I. McFarland before the committee, and that there was nothing crooked then. The word "crooked" is not parliamentary, and I suggest that it be withdrawn.
To say that there was no suggestion of crooked work then is not objectionable.

I do not propose to have words put in my mouth. I said that Mr. McFarland was brought down here, but that there was no suggestion of crooked work. I

said that the operations of the whole grain business was a racket, that it would not bear . investigation, and that we wanted a committee when we came back next fall-it is too late now, of course. We want that committee.
I think it would be satisfactory if the hon. member would state that he made no suggestion of a charge of crookedness against-
He did not make any such suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I request that the official Hansard be produced.

To facilitate matters, and to get on, I made no suggestion of crooked work on the part of these officials. I said that the general grain business was a racket. We know the board has something to do with the operations; they cannot do otherwise. I said that they are dealing with it, and I said, further, that the whole thing would not bear the light of day.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We shall see what the record says.

We shall just let that go. If you will give us a committee-yes, give us a committee; if you will give us a committee and we can call certain witnesses here, we shall see, then. If the Minister of Mines and Resources will not, then just let the Minister of Trade and Commerce say he will give us a committee. Will you give us a committee?
I see no objection whatever.
That is a promise.
I say that I see no objection whatsoever; but I am not speaking for the government.
That is a promise.

I have here a copy of a telegram. I have suggested on several occasions that, in the event of a war being in progress, the government should have taken things over last fall, and operated the grain trade for the duration of the war. I have a copy of a telegram directed to the chairman of the board, and signed by nine members of the grain exchange, namely, N. M. Paterson & Company Limited; McCabe Brothers Grain Company Limited; N. Bawlf Grain Company, Limited; Alberta Pacific Grain Company Limited; Canadian Consolidated Grain Company Limited; Pioneer Grain Company Limited; Western Grain Company Limited; 
Federal Grain Limited, and National Grain Company Limited. It is dated July 18, 1940. In the telegram they review the situation, stating that they know we are in a critical situation, that certain charges had been made in this house that there were exorbitant charges, or money being made unduly. These firms offered their services to the government to operate as agents of the board. They offered their whole systems for the duration of the war on the basis of a 6 per cent earning on capital invested. I have the reply before me of the chairman of the board; he may recall it. The question I wish to ask is: Why did the minister not accept that offer?
The chairman of the board replied:
, Answering telegram from your members as in the past terms of the handling contract for this coming season will be arrived after complete discussion between all companies and our board. Your proposal re operating as agents noted. This has been brought to the attention of the government.
I should like to know why this offer was not accepted? This is the chairman, one of the minister's advisers.
I am now going to review what the situation is at the present time on the grain exchange. If I am not right in what I say., then we shall hear from the minister. There are certain shippers, and grain interests and millers who cannot make delivery of their wheat that is stored in terminals or interior positions. Under their contracts they cannot make delivery, even if they so desired, because they are out of position. Then, there are futures contracts. A lot of it is held by the board, a great amount of it-at least a part of it, anyway, and cash wheat is the remainder. There is a limited capacity at Fort William. This wheat cannot be shipped there to make delivery on their contracts, because the wheat in Fort William is held as options.
Since the board owns most of this, in either options or cash wheat, they cannot take delivery. There is a situation arising there now where the options have to be changed from month to month, and I am informed- and if I am not correctly informed, we shall find out-that the grain firms are in the position similar to that in which they were in 1935, and that they are now negotiating with the wheat board to have their July futures changed into Octobers on a basis of 80 cents for the October. That, of course, would be taking the July as it is now, at about 77J cents, plus storage. That would be about right.
This would commit the wheat boardi to take delivery of wheat in October at or around 80 cents, basis No. 1 northern. Here is what I wish to say, that if that deal is going on

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
now, it should be confined to the 1941 crop, and there should be a price of 80 cents; the 70 cents should be increased to 80 cents. If the board is now making a settlement with the grain firtns on a basis of 80 cents for October wheat, when the wheat is supposed to have been taken at 70 cents, then we, the producers, should receive 80 cents for the 1941 crop. If that arrangement is going on- and we can find out whether it is correct or not-and we know that the board controls all wheat, either by options or cash, then if they are making that settlement with the grain firms, I say that it should apply to the 1941 crop for the farmers. That is the situation. I say that we should have the price fixed higher.
Here is another point to which I should like briefly to refer. I may say that since yesterday-

I must remind the hon. gentleman
that he has spoken for forty minutes.
I should be glad to have the hon. gentleman proceed.
Go on.

I am going to refer to
something mentioned yesterday by the leader of the opposition, the shipment of wheat to Japan. I want the minister to follow me, and perhaps he can give us some more information. I made inquiries about this, as well as about the situation to which I have just referred. In connection with the shipment of wheat to Japan I am informed that the Canadian exporters, James Richardson and Sons, the Reliance Grain company and three others would have nothing to do with this deal. This shipment was made by the Continental Grain company, the Dreyfus company and the Bunge company, three international Jew firms. The Dreyfus company has since been changed to the Leval company.

I
think I should correct the statement the hon. gentleman has just made. He has stated that this shipment was made by three
companies.
International companies.
The Canada Grain company of Vancouver, a well known Canadian firm, handled this shipment of wheat.

Were they the agents or the principals?
14873-231}
They were the principals.
What is the evidence of that? I have other evidence.

I
am giving the information asked for. This is a Canadian company headed by Mr. McKee, a prominent resident of Vancouver.

I have been informed on
good authority that these three companies figured in this deal and that the two companies I have named refused to have anything to do with it. These other companies are international companies. I am informed also that grain is always shipped in bulk to Japan or China, and that the fact that this shipment was in bags is evidence that it was intended for Russia or for enemy hands, to be reached through Russia.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We have heard that before.

These international grain
firms should not be permitted to do business with the grain board, and the grain board should not deliver a single bushel of wheat to them.

I
have just denied the transaction.

These are not loyal Canadian firms, and therefore the board should not deal with them in any way, shape or form. An investigation should be held into this sale in order to find out if these firms had anything to do with it. This investigation should, also cover the taxes paid by these firms and just what their capital investment is. I understand that these firms cover up their tax returns by showing the business they are doing in other countries as well as in Canada. They are evading their taxes, and this should be investigated.
The policy adopted by the board for the coming season has not met with the approval of the western producer. When the proper time comes, the minister will have to answer other questions with respect to the board's operations. I think I have produced sufficient evidence to-night to warrant the government in taking over the whole business. If that is done there will be no possibility of the things I have mentioned happening in the future.

I do not intend to speak at any length, but there are one or two observations I should like to make in connection with our wheat marketing, coming as I do from a province where wheat has been king for a number of years. As the hon. member

Sup-ply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) stated, there is dissatisfaction with the price and with the operations of the grain exchange.
I am going to ask the minister, first, to clear up a point which I raised the other evening with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). It has been stated in various parts of western Canada, as well as to myself, that the wheat board is assisting a number of grain operators on the grain exchange on a relief basis. The statement is made that the board is allowing these men sufficient business in the way of spreading options from month to month or from period to period to give them about $150 a month. If that statement is not true, this is the place where it should be cleared up. If it is true, the practice should be discontinued. With the situation as it is among our farming population, with low prices and no prospect of better conditions, the farmers feel that their industry should not be used to maintain operators who are part of an organization which they have fought for a good many years. I am referring to the Winnipeg grain exchange. As the minister knows, there is a widespread feeling among the farmers of western Canada that the grain exchange should be closed.
Then there is the other matter of storage referred to by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. It is unnecessary to traverse the points he made because he presented them very clearly indeed. But our farmers are uneasy about the future; they wonder what the policy is going to be next year. They feel that if storage is required, they can build satisfactory weather-proof bins, and with the prices at their present depressed levels, they should be entitled to receive adequate storage charges. A return was brought down a short time ago showing that one grain company had rented a government terminal elevator at a rental of $51,000. On the basis of the minimum use of that elevator, the storage charges will give that company a revenue roughly five times that amount. Under certain circumstances, that revenue might be increased considerably, in which event the rent would be increased to some extent. But the revelation which was given wide publicity in western Canada has certainly not tended to give confidence to farmers of the west when they see a parliamentary return indicating a rental of that description and payment for storage in the neighbourhood of the figure I have mentioned. Some consideration should be given to that problem.
We as a group thoroughly endorse the request which was made early in the session and repeated in a few words to-night by the the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-I do not
MMr. roldweU.J
know whether he represents his entire party in that regard-that the whole elevator system in the country should be taken over under
the War Measures Act at least for the duration of the war, and that there should be no private gain in connection with the elevator service. The hon. member for Wood Mountain last year discussed the amounts that were paid in storage. I was not sure that his figures were altogether correct, but even if they were not, his statement revealed a storage condition which is most alarming to those of us who wish to see the producers get from their industry all that it is possible for them to get, particularly at this time.
There are a number of questions which will come up under individual items of the estimates, and I do not propose to ask a series of questions now, particularly because some of our members have various questions to ask. I do, however, wish to place ourselves clearly on record that we think, first that the government of Canada under the circumstances which now exist, with vast accumulations of grain in our country, which are likely to remain in our country, should undertake to see that this tremendous accumulation of wheat is carried in the most economical way. The government has endeavoured this year to cut down the production of wheat, and incidentally the farmers responded better than I thought they would in reducing their acreage. But with the moisture conditions which now exist in western Canada, and with a good month in June and a few showers in July, we may actually, even with the reduced acreage, hatm a bigger crop this year than we had last year. With that possibility facing us, these tremendous accumulations of wheat, I repeat, should be carried in the most economical way possible and to the benefit of the producers rather than of the grain companies. I am certain that I speak for a very large number of people when I say that in order to do that, the entire elevator system in this country should be taken over by the government at least for the duration of the war, or, in the alternative, until we can dispose of these large accumulations. Then a further policy regarding the elevator and storage system of Canada can be decided upon through this parliament.
Second, I am of the very firm opinion that the grain exchange to-day performs no useful function. There was a time when we had long arguments here as to the advantages of spreading options month after month or period after period because it was suggested that was an economical way of carrying grain over. As Mr. Mclvor's predecessor once

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
suggested to the parliamentary committee on wheat in 1936, it was a way of spreading the speculative losses over the largest number of people. The little speculators in those days were the people who took the losses; that is the interpretation I placed on his remarks, and that I think is true. At the present time there is no considerable trading on our grain exchange, and there seems to be no good reason why the exchange should be kept open.
One other thing I would like to say, and this is an endorsement and perhaps a repetition. Our group for a number of years has protested against the sending of munitions and supplies to potential aggressor nations, and I certainly was surprised when, after the government had stated a policy last year of preventing supplies of various kinds going to a possible enemy-and Japan now certainly is that without a doubt-I learned that we have just lately loaded a very large shipment of wheat to go to Japan. Of course it is said that it is only on Japanese account, that the wheat is going to China. But it is going to Japanese-controlled China in any event, and there is a possibility that either the shipment itself, or by replacing some other supplies, may eventually benefit our principal enemy, Germany. I certainly think the time has arrived when we should ship nothing to a possible aggressor. We may be at war with Japan at any time. As we know, she is threatening the Dutch East Indies to-day, and if that threat is carried out there will be war with Japan in a very short time. One of the reasons why I was so critical of the policies of the governments leading up to this war, one of the reasons why I feared that the democratic nations which were continuing this policy were not interested in maintaining democracy but that they might even be found on the side of the aggressor nations eventually, was the fact that we continued all through the pre-war years to ship supplies to countries which were ultimately going to use them to destroy us. We are following that policy now when we ship supplies to Japan. We have a fairly good excuse for not doing so because we have no control over that part of China. We have not a friendly government in that part of China to which the wheat is being shipped. Therefore I wish to endorse the principle that the wheat ought not to have been allowed to be shipped, and I hope that certainly no further sales of that kind will be made.
There are other matters I wish to bring up on individual items of the estimates as we come to them, but with these general remarks I shall leave the matter to-night.

I shall confine myself
to-night largely to general remarks. First of all, on behalf of this group I protest against the shipment of grain to Japan. I was amazed when I heard that that is being done. I do not see how we can expect a really united war effort in this country so long as transactions of that kind are being carried on. It would be bad enough if the real destination of this grain was Japan, but apparently it is being shipped to Japan in transit to other countries which, if not our actual enemies to-day, at least are potential enemies.
In the past we have laid down what we considered to be a sound policy in regard to wheat, and I shall not take much time to-night to refer to that. We have stressed the fact that we consider the price of 70 cents a bushel altogether too low. We have pointed out that that policy has been largely responsible for building up the great surpluses which we have because farmers have been compelled to increase their operations in an attempt to reduce their overhead. We have suggested that a price of SI a bushel for a limited delivery, with a minimum of 1,500 bushels graded upwards, should have been put in operation.
We have also urged on many occasions that the grain exchange should be closed because we do not believe it is performing any useful or necessary function at this time.
We have urged the government to take over all grain-handling facilities in order to do away with the very heavy storage charges *Which have to be paid during the war.
Another point which I believe is important is that regarding an advance against grain in storage on the farm. The minister himself has admitted that it is possible we may only be able to have an initial quota of two or three bushels to the acre instead of five. If that is so, I am wondering how the farmers will be able to carry on this fall.

I
would not want the idea to go out to the country that either the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the government or the wheat board suggested that only two or three bushels would be taken on the first quota from the 1941 crop. The intention is that it will be five, but a great deal will depend upon the condition with regard to available space at the time.	.

I understand that, but the
figure "five" was mentioned. The minister will agree; however, that under certain circumstances it may be possible to give only two or three, and even at five bushels to the acre, if a farmer has a crop of thirty or forty

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
bushels, he will not be able to pay his threshing expenses if he can deliver only five bushels. It is essential that advances should be made against the grain in storage so that the farmer can at least pay the actual cash operating expenses. I have here, order in council P.C. 3849 containing what I presume are the latest regulations, and I confess I find it difficult to know just where we are, because there have been so manj^ orders in council, one cancelling the other, that unless we have the very latest we are out of date. I thought all this time I knew what the regulations were, regarding acreage bonus, but I find another one has recently been passed which entirely changes the picture.
There is just one in this case.

There is only one in so
far as these regulations are concerned, and section 17 reads:
Wherever a quota of the grain produced on any land becomes deliverable, any producer entitled to a definite share of the crop as landlord, vendor or mortgagee, shall be entitled to have delivered in his name a share of such quota proportionate to such person's said interest in the grain, and shall have equal rights of delivery accorded to producers under the act. . . .
Does that mean that out of his five bushels delivered the farmer will be able to get only a portion for himself, and that the mortgage company will have a portion and the landlord a portion? Surely it means that. I should like to be corrected if I am wrong.

The farmer will have the permit. Let me quote:
. . . for such purpose the permit holder shall make the permit available, but the enforcement of this provision shall be the direct concern and responsibility of the interested parties themselves and no legal obligation shall devolve on the board in respect thereto.

But that does not alter
the situation. It merely means that the board itself is not taking legal responsibility for enforcing it. The fact remains that the provision is there which compels the farmer to divide his quota with certain interested parties.

The farmer will have the permit, and he will get delivery.
_ Mr. QUELCH: According to section 17, it is supposed to be divided among the various parties. The board will not assume the legal responsibility of enforcing the provisions, but through the courts these other people can insist upon a share of the quota being delivered to them., According to section 17, the farmer
[Mr. QuelchJ
can be compelled by law to deliver a certain portion of the five bushels to the mortgage company and the landlord, and I suggest that it will be hard enough for him to carry on with five bushels.

Has that not
always been the law?

No, it has not always been
the law. The farmer has not been compelled to deliver only five bushels to the acre.
I am referring to the proportions that are delivered.

Yes; but the farmer has not formerly been in the position where he has been able to deliver only five bushels, or possibly two or three. He has been able to deliver the whole crop. Out of the five bushels he will have to pay his threshing bill, so that if a man threshes forty bushels to the acre, five bushels will not cover that expenditure.
How could he get by last year?
Last year he was allowed to keep the whole five bushels.
Who allowed him?
He had a special permit, and the five was quickly increased in the heavy producing districts to ten to the acre. In the Morrin district, the five was increased to eight almost immediately.
Who allowed the farmer to retain the five bushels to the acre?
The provincial government at that time took steps to guarantee the farmer's retention of the first quota.
And only the provincial government can do it.

I
have here a long statement which I intend to put on Hansard on another occasion with an accompanying explanation, but first I wish to deal with a large number of categorical questions that have been asked me to-night.
